#9477. Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial

A new approach to treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has received FDA clearance, offering a personalized alternative for people who have not found sufficient relief through existing treatments. Developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, the technology uses brain activity measurements to guide targeted magnetic stimulation.

Early clinical trial findings have been encouraging. According to Wave Neuroscience, patients experienced a 52% reduction in PTSD symptoms, while 68% achieved remission. The full findings are still being prepared for public release, but researchers believe the technology could significantly expand treatment options for millions of people.

The need for more effective PTSD care is substantial. In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day, and about 7% of veterans receive a PTSD diagnosis annually.

PTSD can develop after traumatic experiences such as military combat, serious accidents, natural disasters, or violence. An estimated 6% of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans.

Why Current PTSD Treatments Are Not Enough

Since PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980, treatment has largely centered on psychotherapy and medications known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), including sertraline and fluoxetine.

Although these approaches can help, many patients continue to experience symptoms despite receiving treatment.

A 2020 review of PTSD medications found that patients reported improvements ranging from 6.8 to 10.1 points on symptom assessments. However, remission rates reached only 10.9% at most.

Wave Neuroscience reported substantially stronger preliminary outcomes in its clinical trial. Erik Won, DO, the company's chief medical officer, described the results as a major advance over previously reported medication outcomes.

“In comparison to that study, our FDA trial reported a 52% reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” Won said. “And more importantly, we saw 68% remission in our clinical trial. So, it’s really a quantum change, an inflection point in what we can offer to patients. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.”

These findings are promising, although the results come from different studies and should not be interpreted as a direct comparison of treatment effectiveness.

The newly cleared system uses Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), a technology that combines measurements of brain activity with targeted magnetic stimulation.

First, an electroencephalogram (EEG) records the brain's electrical signals. This information helps guide a personalized treatment plan using transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS.

During TMS, a coil positioned against the scalp delivers magnetic pulses that stimulate brain activity. The technique has already been used for other psychiatric conditions, including treatment-resistant depression.

What distinguishes MeRT is its use of an AI-assisted algorithm to customize stimulation protocols based on each patient's brain activity rather than relying on a standardized approach.

“Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, was previously FDA cleared for treatment-resistant depression,” Won said. “By adding an augmented AI derived multivariate algorithm, we were able to personalize protocols that received FDA clearance for post-traumatic stress disorder, which should open up market access to about 13 million people who may be struggling with PTSD.”

Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a physician-scientist at Texas A&M Health with extensive experience in precision medicine, helped guide the research.

His work focuses on adapting medical care to the characteristics of individual patients instead of assuming that everyone will respond to the same treatment.

“Most clinical interventions for the treatment of PTSD do not work very well,” Ramos said. “So, this is a huge area where identifying interventions that could hopefully add quality of life to the people impacted by this disorder would be tremendously impactful.”

Wave Neuroscience CEO Fred Walke said Ramos was a natural fit for the project because of his expertise in personalized medicine.

Conventional TMS generally follows treatment protocols that are less individualized. MeRT builds on the same underlying technology but adjusts treatment according to the patient's specific brain activity.

Ramos emphasized that even small biological differences between people can have major implications for medical care. Humans are approximately 99.9% genetically alike, yet the remaining 0.1% contributes to differences that can influence how individuals respond to treatment.

By accounting for these differences and tailoring stimulation to each person's brain, researchers observed substantial reductions in PTSD symptom severity.

Ramos illustrated the distinction with an analogy involving a leaking roof.

He likened conventional TMS to covering a leak with a tarp to manage its effects. MeRT, in contrast, aims to provide a more targeted solution, comparable to identifying and replacing the damaged shingles responsible for the problem.

The broader goal is to move beyond treating patients with standardized protocols and toward interventions guided by measurable biological information.

From Breakthrough Designation to FDA Clearance

The regulatory process reached an important milestone in 2024, when MeRT received an FDA Breakthrough Device designation.

Dr. Rick Silva, executive director of clinical trials at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, explained that the designation helps promising technologies move through regulatory review more efficiently.

It does not eliminate scientific or medical requirements. Instead, it can streamline communication and reduce administrative delays while preserving the standards needed for FDA clearance.

Silva said the progress was particularly meaningful because the project began during the COVID-19 pandemic and advanced through the regulatory process unusually quickly.

According to Silva, medical device development and clinical evaluation can often take around 10 years before clearance is obtained. This project completed the relevant process in just over two years.

He credited the experience and dedication of the Wave Neuroscience team with helping make that accelerated progress possible.

“I’ve been involved in probably close to 1,000 projects in academic medical centers over the years at varying degrees of depth and detail,” Silva said. “Patients are why I do what I do. It’s hard, and the failure rate is high, and it’s a lot of work. But when you get to a point where something is going to benefit patients, it’s very professionally gratifying and personally gratifying in many ways as well.”

Dr. Israel Liberzon, distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, served as the study's lead psychiatrist and PTSD specialist.

He believes the clearance represents an important expansion of the available treatments for PTSD.

According to Liberzon, MeRT will become the only FDA-cleared nonmedication treatment specifically for PTSD once it reaches patients.

“Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” Liberzon said. “It doesn’t mean that only two of them are used, but both are SSRIs. This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.”

In the clinical trial, participants received five treatment sessions each week over a period of five to six weeks.

Researchers reported that the improvements appeared to persist after the treatment sessions ended, suggesting the benefits may extend beyond the active therapy period.

For patients who struggle with medication side effects or find psychotherapy difficult to complete, a treatment based on personalized brain stimulation could provide another option.

“People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.”

Won also believes the technology could eventually be adapted to other psychiatric conditions, including depression and anxiety.

Could Personalized Brain Therapy Transform Mental Healthcare?

Dr. Leslie S. Prichep, chief scientific officer at Wave Neuroscience, sees the FDA clearance as an important step toward treatment decisions guided by objective measurements of brain function.

“The FDA clearance of the MeRT System reflects decades of scientific research using electrophysiological biomarkers in identifying abnormal brain activity profiles and guiding personalized intervention strategies,” Prichep said. “We believe this represents an important advancement toward a more objective, data-informed model of mental healthcare.”

Walke believes that giving patients clearer information about their brain activity could also help change public attitudes toward mental illness.

He compared the idea to treating a broken bone with a cast. By making mental health conditions easier to understand through measurable physical information, the company hopes to reduce stigma and help patients better understand their experiences.

“One of the goals of the company is to create a platform for mental healthcare that uses objective imagery to help patients understand why they’re experiencing life the way that they are,” Walke said. “That insight, compounded with proven technologies, promises incredibly high efficacy when personalized.”

An important next step will be ensuring that patients can actually obtain the treatment. Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working with other stakeholders to expand availability and make the therapy more affordable through insurance coverage.

“Our hope is that this research and technology can be a catalyst for more widespread development and innovation of more effective, personalized and precision-guided treatments,” Won said. “This is proof positive that population-scale personalized medicine is not just an aspirational goal but is an achievable reality today.”

The project combines years of work across medicine, neuroscience, clinical research, and technology, all directed toward improving the lives of people affected by PTSD.

For Ramos, the opportunity to help veterans carries particular significance because of Texas A&M's longstanding involvement in military and veteran initiatives.

“Texas A&M has a very rich history of military and veteran priorities,” Ramos said. “It’s a no-brainer that Texas A&M faculty would be interested in and supportive of an initiative that hopefully would bring positive solutions to a big problem. And anything we could do to help alleviate that problem is going to go a long way towards making a difference in the individual’s life as well as the people who are close to them. I feel very fortunate that we at Texas A&M were meaningfully involved in this project.”

Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Lasha Markham. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9476. As protests in Georgia intensify again, a new private museum puts focus on the country’s artists

The dramatic new home of the Kvareli Foundation (right) sits in countryside around 150km east of the Tbilisi Courtesy Midamo

Georgia’s art scene has been navigating a period of tension since a wave of protests rippled through the country in 2024, sparked by issues including the introduction of a law that critics say threatens freedom of expression. Two years on, as demonstrations continue, some much-needed good news for local artists has arrived with the launch of a new private museum dedicated to Georgian contemporary art.

The Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, around two hours’ drive east from Tbilisi, past fields, forts and mountains, is scheduled to open on 2 November. One of its core missions, according to the foundation’s creative director Nino Sulkhanishvili, is “to show the artists who aren’t given space in an institutional setting”, in some cases because of their political stances. “We decided to give the space to those who actually need it,” she says.

The institution has been built from scratch on 115 acres of land purchased by its founder, the shipping and logistics executive Jemal Inaishvili. It is housed in a hyper-modern two-storey building, its facade a series of blood-red slats encased in a silver-grey frame.

Along with the exhibition spaces and shop, there is a rooftop auditorium for performances and film screenings. “We wish to have many reasons to have good people come and celebrate,” Inaishvili says. The grounds also comprise sculptures, a five-star hotel and a winery. The estimated total cost is more than €25m, funded by Inaishvili and his family.

An aerial view of the foundation, showing its rooftop space that will be used for performances and film screenings

Inaishvili’s personal collection provides an anchor for the foundation’s programme. He has been amassing art for about 40 years: he thought of becoming a painter in his youth, he explains, and surrounded himself with artists. He recalls the incident that kickstarted his collecting: “It was around 1985 and we were drinking until late hours. The artist Irakli Sutidze was hosting us and I said: ‘I want to buy this work’”. From the mid-1990s onwards, contemporary art became his focus.

It was a time of challenge and opportunity, Inaishvili says: following Georgia’s independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, “the country was poor, and so there were not too many buyers, not too many collectors”. Today, he remains one of few major collectors in the country who is concentrated on the work of living artists—something he wishes to change through his foundation. About 10% of his collection is by international artists–including Ukrainians, whom he is keen to support, he says, “especially in this very, very difficult condition for their nation”.

The inaugural exhibition, Georgian Contemporary Art: Origins and Continuities, combines works from Inaishvili’s collection with loans to trace the development of Georgian art since the 1960s. It will show, for example, how “in the post-Stalin era, artists began to experiment with their autonomy”, Sulkhanishvili explains; and how, in the 1970s and 1980s, artists began to work together in conscious opposition to art sanctioned by the Soviets, with examples including the avant-garde collective Archivarius. It will also explore the work of artists like Misha Shengelia and Kote Sulaberidze, who incorporated dark humour into their work in the 1990s to express their experiences of a difficult time for many Georgians, marked by war and financial chaos.

Courtesy of Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art

Inaishvili says this whole story has never been told before. But “we’re not trying to show everything that was done during those times,” Sulkhanishvili says, adding that the exhibition will feature many works that have never been seen in public.

“I was trying to see, first of all, what is the definition of contemporary art in general—so how Modernism developed into Post-modernism and contemporary art,” he says. “I tried to fix that equation in Georgian art, which was difficult because everything was basically underground, unofficial practice.”

Courtesy of Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art

Georgia’s institutional art sector has only been developing in earnest, Sulkhanishvili says, since the early 2000s. This has been a complicated journey, defined by seismic political shifts including the current Georgian Dream government’s pivot away from Europe and towards Russia.

The adoption of the so-called “Russian law”—officially the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence—in spring 2024 ushered in new rules for organisations receiving foreign funding, which the NGO Human Rights Watch argued would “marginalise and stifle critical voices”. The move prompted crowds of creative workers to take to the streets and boycott public institutions. Disputed parliamentary results in October that year, and the Georgian government’s decision to suspend EU accession talks a month later, brought fresh, intensified protests.

These demonstrations have continued since. This month, amid outcry over a lawsuit brought by Georgian Dream that seeks to ban five opposition parties, a new campaign was launched, which is reportedly expected to culminate with a major rally on 28 November.

The fractious relationship between artists and state institutions places emphasis on the role of independent organisations like the Kvareli Foundation. Inaishvili’s career has been primarily in the shipping and logistics sector; his current roles include chairman of the board of Tbilisi Dry Port. But he also served as a member of the Georgian parliament—for his home constituency of Batumi—and as the deputy chair of parliament in the early 2000s, during Mikheil Saakashvili’s presidency. Business, he says, has always been his main focus. “If I wanted to continue in politics, I would still be in it; I said, ‘thank you and goodbye’.”

Sulkhanishvili places emphasis not just on the foundation’s independence but also its location outside of Tbilisi, which, she says, already has a healthy ecosystem of commercial galleries as well as foundations such as Atinati.

“Our goal is to shift the focus from the capital,” she says. “Kakheti [the wider region in which Kvareli is located] is known for its hospitality, its wine, for its amazing food, for its amazing historical sites, but not specifically for contemporary art. This is something that’s never been brought before.” There are plans for a future residency programme at the institution.

Inaishvili says he wishes to help people—including the country’s wealthy and international visitors—to learn about Georgian contemporary art and perhaps inspire them to collect and patronise it, as he has been doing for four decades. “Georgian artists do not have enough support in my opinion,” he says. “We have to create the appetite.”

#9475. Ten Data-Backed Truths Of User Experience ROI

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In the high-stakes economy of today, the cost of a friction-heavy interface is no longer just “lost clicks”, but potentially millions in wasted engineering spend and lost business value. As a veteran UX designer who has helped build digital products since the early mobile-first era, I’ve watched business leaders shift from viewing design as a “cosmetic preference” to recognising that user experience is actually the primary engine of business survival.

A UX design role is as much about research and analytics as it is about pixels, and I believe that hard data is the only tool powerful enough to bridge the gap between design and the boardroom. Facts don’t just advocate for the user; they prove that UX is a non-negotiable requirement for a healthy bottom line. Even in the rooms where decisions are made, UX is frequently undervalued as a ‘visual’ role. I’ve learned that the most effective way to dismantle this myth is through data.

The following ten facts represent the current reality of the digital world. These are not just “design tips”; they are the clinical, data-backed pillars for financial growth in a saturated market. Some of these facts are also commonly used by designers as best practices.

For example, I once led a B2C mobile design project, where I was able to strip 1.2 seconds off the mobile load time by reducing and removing some of the visual assets. The result was an immediate 12% lift in completed transactions, proving that in UX, every tenth of a second is a direct lever for revenue.

One of the most compelling financial arguments for UX is the 1:100 rule. Modern studies, such as from the IBM Systems Institute and Sugue Technologies, show that fixing an error after a product has been developed and launched can be up to 100 times more expensive than fixing it during the initial design and prototyping phase.

Think of UX as “engineering insurance.” By the time a developer touches the code, every interaction should have been validated. If you discover a fundamental navigation flaw after launch, you aren’t just paying for the fix; you’re paying for technical debt, lost developer time, and the revenue lost while users struggle with a broken flow.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

In the current landscape, performance is the essential foundation of user experience. A beautiful interface is worthless if the user bounces before it renders. The data is uncompromising: 47% of users expect a page to load in two seconds or less, and missing this window is a financial catastrophe. A mere one-second delay can reduce conversions by 20% and satisfaction by 16%, while retail businesses lose an estimated $2.6 billion annually to slow load times. When mobile load time moves from one to three seconds, the bounce rate spikes by 32%, and by the third second, conversion rates typically plummet from 40% to 29%.

However, this volatility offers a massive lever for growth. Even a microscopic 0.1-second improvement can lift retail conversions by 8.4%, and travel site conversions by 10.1%. Improving your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) by 31% — a benchmark 67% of websites achieved as of June 2025 — can drive a direct 8% increase in sales. As a long-time designer, I treat speed as a primary design element.

First impressions are both visceral and aesthetic. Research indicates that users form an opinion about a website’s visual appeal in approximately 50 milliseconds (0.05 seconds). That’s not a lot of time! This split-second “gut-feeling” is a survival mechanism that dictates whether a user stays to explore your value proposition or bounces immediately.

In the current market, 94% of first impressions are strictly design related. If your interface feels “off” or dated, users subconsciously project that lack of quality onto your entire product or service. Your content effectively doesn’t exist if your design hasn’t earned the five seconds of attention required to read it.

Stakeholders often think “more options” equals “more value.” Psychology proves the opposite. Hick’s Law states that the time it takes to make a decision increases with the number of options available.

Every extra menu item or form field is a “tax” on the user’s brain. As noted by Landbase, top-performing sites now achieve conversion rates exceeding 11%, while average performers struggle below 3%. Those performing well have applied personalization and optimization strategies to simplify the experience.

“White space” is often viewed as wasted real estate by non-designers. In reality, it is a tool for focus. Strategic use of white space can increase a user’s content comprehension by up to 20%.

White space prevents “cognitive load” from peaking. By giving the user’s eyes a place to rest, you guide them toward the most important elements, usually your “Buy” or “Sign Up” button. In 2026, as attention spans have dropped to roughly 8 seconds, simplicity is the ultimate luxury and a major driver of engagement.

For example, in a fintech dashboard I worked on, analyst users were feeling overwhelmed by a ‘data dump’ layout in some of the dashboard components. I applied more white space around the data to lower their cognitive load. Simply giving the data room to breathe led to a 25% decrease in time-on-task and a significant boost in trial-to-paid conversions.

One of the most surprising psychological hacks in UX is that users will complete a task faster if they believe they have already made progress. This is known as the Goal Gradient Effect.

In a classic study, researchers found that a 10-stamp coffee card with two stamps already “pre-filled” was completed significantly faster than an 8-stamp card with zero pre-fills, even though the total spend required was identical. In digital design, showing a progress bar that starts at 15% (simply for creating an account) increases completion rates for onboarding by over 40%. We aren’t just designing screens — we are managing the user’s dopamine and sense of momentum.

Many stakeholders believe that cramming more text “above the fold” increases value. Data proves the opposite. Proper typography, specifically line spacing (leading) and paragraph width, can increase content comprehension and reading speed by up to 20%.

Optimal line height (generally 1.5x the font size) reduces “visual noise,” allowing the brain to process information with less cognitive effort. When users struggle to read your text due to tight spacing or small fonts, their “perceived effort” increases, leading to a higher bounce rate. Legibility is a conversion tool: if it’s hard to read, it’s hard to buy.

There are many ways to display more legible text. For example, if line spacing (leading) is too small or the font is too heavy, this also impacts readability.

This truth meshes well with the previous one. Users do not read your website; they scan it. On a typical web page, users read only about 20% to 28% of the text.

Because modern users scan in an F-pattern or Spotted pattern, designing for reading is a tactical error. We must design for scanning.

I have heard of companies that waste six-figure budgets on massive user studies with 100 people, only to get buried in noise. The reality is that testing with just 5 users typically uncovers 85% of usability problems.

This is a mathematical sweet spot. After the fifth user, you reach the point of diminishing returns — you spend more money to find fewer new bugs. The competitive advantage belongs to small and frequent user testing activities. Test with 5 people, iterate, and test with 5 more. It is the most cost-effective way to build a bulletproof product.

Personally, I have followed this guideline many times during user testing activities, and I can confidently say that testing with 5 people does deliver the majority of issues in your design.

Last, but definitely not least, the most staggering statistic in our industry remains consistent. On average, every $1 invested in UX returns $100. This 9,900% ROI isn’t magic, but the sum of increased conversion and reduced support.

A fully optimised UX design can improve conversion rates by up to 400%. Furthermore, intuitive design significantly lowers customer support requirements. When a product is self-explanatory, you don’t need a massive call centre to explain how to use it.

Beyond these individual statistics, we must address the cumulative effect of a mature UX practice. In my years of practising, the most successful firms are those that treat UX as a continuous improvement loop rather than a one-off project. The data shows that companies with high design maturity see 32% higher revenue growth and 56% higher total returns to shareholders compared to their less design-focused peers.

This discrepancy exists because mature UX organisations move beyond “user delight” and into “user efficiency.” When you shave 30 seconds off a workflow for a team of 1,000 employees, you aren’t just making them happier; you are reclaiming hundreds of thousands of dollars in annual productivity. This internal ROI is often overlooked, but it is just as vital as consumer-facing conversion rates.

Furthermore, the “experience gap” is real. 80% of companies believe they deliver a “superior experience,” but only 8% of customers agree. This massive disconnect represents a significant market opportunity for those willing to look at the hard data. By bridging this gap through continuous user testing and performance optimisation, you aren’t just improving a product but capturing market share that your competitors are leaving on the table.

Today, we cannot talk about UX without talking about AI. However, AI hasn’t replaced these 10 facts, but it has accelerated the solution on some of these.

AI has turned UX from a static map into a living, breathing guide for users. But the fundamental rules of human psychology, such as our 50ms judgments and our need for white space, remain unchanged.

In summary, here is a list of the key truths to remember:

As we move deeper into the late 2020s, the line between “design” and “business strategy” has vanished. The data is in, and companies that lead in design outperform their competitors by 1.7x in revenue growth.

UX design is no longer a team you hire to “make things look nice.” It is the research-driven, data-backed discipline that ensures your digital product isn’t just a cost centre, but a revenue-generating machine.

In fact, this has always been the case, but I hope that in presenting these cold, hard truths, it now becomes a reality for your business.

As I have found over the years, implementing factual design improvements does make a difference that intuition alone can’t replicate. We are past the era of subjective opinions. The data is clear, the psychology is proven, and the ROI is undeniable. The only question left is whether you’re ready to let the facts lead your design, or if you’ll let your competitors do it first.

#9474. Advanced Tree Counting: Mathematical Layouts With `sibling-index()` And `sibling-count()`

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

You know that thing where you have a grid of cards, and you want them to fade in one after another? That staggered cascade effect. Looks great. Should be simple. And yet every time I’ve built it, the implementation has made me feel like I’m doing something fundamentally stupid.

See the Pen [Dynamic Staggered Animations with CSS sibling-index() [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/zxowBog) by Durgesh.

Because the options were always the same. Say you want staggered animation delays on a list of 10 items. You either wrote a Sass loop that spat out a dozen :nth-child() rules, each one hardcoding a --index variable for that specific position:

Ten items. Ten rules. If the list grows to 50? You cap it and hope for the best, or set up a Sass loop that generates hundreds of selectors at build time. Engineers like Roman Komarov have come up with O(âˆšN) strategies — legitimately clever stuff — but you still end up with 63 rules to cover 1,023 elements.

Or you looped through elements in JavaScript and set inline styles. style="--index: 3". Right there in the DOM. Works fine. Also spreads layout concerns across your scripts and quietly breaks six months later when someone refactors the component without realizing the CSS depends on a JavaScript-injected variable.

Both approaches have always bugged me for the same reason: you’re telling the browser something it already knows. The browser built the DOM tree. It knows which element is the third child. It has the data. CSS just couldn’t access it.

One line. Works for 5 items or 5,000. No event listeners. No mutation observers. No re-renders.

sibling-index() and sibling-count() are part of the CSS Values and Units Module Level 5 spec (Section 9, if you’re the type who reads W3C drafts for fun). The proposal was approved via CSSWG issue #4559 after substantial discussion. The functions themselves take no arguments — you just use them.

Both functions resolve to — not , an actual number. That means you can throw them into calc(), min(), max(), round(), mod(), trigonometric stuff like sin() and cos(). When you write calc(sibling-index() * 100ms), CSS handles the type coercion and spits out a valid value. No tricks needed. Compare that with counter(), which returns a string and can only live inside content on pseudo-elements — it’s a different thing entirely.

One clarification that trips people up: :nth-child() is a selector. It picks elements. It doesn’t produce a value. You can’t write calc(:nth-child() * 10px) — that’s not valid CSS. sibling-index() does the opposite. It sits inside your declarations and gives you a number you can calculate with. They solve different problems, and until now we’ve been duct-taping :nth-child() into a role it was never designed for.

Once it clicks that these are just integers, ideas come fast.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

Want the last item to animate first? Subtract:

Last child gets (N - N) * 80ms = 0ms — it fires instantly. First child gets (N - 1) * 80ms. The animation kicks off the moment the page loads instead of pausing for an awkward beat.

Stop counting children manually to set percentages:

Five tabs? 20% each. Add a sixth? 16.66%. Remove two? 25%. No media queries, no resize observers, no JavaScript at all.

That said, you can imagine a scenario where too many items make for really narrow tabs, at which point you might want to go with something else, perhaps a Flexbox wrapping solution.

Spread colors evenly across the color wheel:

Three items get hues 120Â° apart. Twelve items get 30Â° increments. The palette adapts to whatever’s in the DOM, which is the kind of thing you’d normally reach for a JavaScript color library to do.

Distributing items in a circle used to mean calculating sine and cosine in JavaScript. CSS now has sin() and cos() natively (Juan Diego RodrÃ­guez has a great practical walkthrough of these on CSS-Tricks), and combined with tree-counting, the whole thing collapses into pure CSS:

Six items? Hexagon. Eight? Octagon. Add or remove items, and the layout recalculates. No JavaScript computing coordinates.

First card stacks highest, last card gets 0. Flip the math if you want the reverse.

These are worth going through individually because they’re not obvious from the spec.

sibling-index() and sibling-count() operate on the DOM tree, not the flattened visual tree. This distinction will absolutely bite you with Web Components.

Say you have a custom element with this shadow DOM:

If you style .internal with sibling-index(), it returns 2. Always. Even if the projects 300 elements. The function sees two children of

in the shadow tree — the and the .internal div. Projected light DOM content doesn’t exist as far as the count is concerned.

There’s also a security thing going on here. If a light DOM stylesheet tries to reach into a component via ::part() and use sibling-index(), the browser returns 0. Flat zero. It’s a deliberate wall to prevent external CSS from probing the internal structure of third-party components. Honestly, I think that’s the right call.

::before and ::after aren’t siblings. They don’t show up in sibling-count() and they don’t have their own sibling-index(). But — and this is the part that’ll save you a debugging session — you can use these functions inside pseudo-element declarations. When you write #target::before { width: calc(sibling-index() * 10px); }, it evaluates sibling-index() against #target, not against the pseudo-element. The pseudo-element isn’t a real node, so the function traces back to its originating element. Same story with ::slotted(*)::before — it checks the slotted element’s index in the light DOM.

This one burned me. Elements with display: none vanish from the layout tree. They take up no space. Screen readers don’t see them. But they’re still in the DOM.

Since sibling-index() reads the DOM tree, not the layout tree, hidden elements get counted:

Cherry is 3, not 2. The hidden banana still holds its spot.

This doesn’t matter for most layouts. But if you’re building something like a search filter that hides non-matching items with display: none, your staggered animations and circular layouts will develop gaps. The visible items keep their original, non-sequential indexes. For anything that depends on continuous counting — radial menus, proportional widths — you’ll need to actually remove filtered nodes from the DOM instead of just hiding them. Or fall back to JavaScript-managed indexes.

Note: visibility: hidden and opacity: 0 count too, but that feels more intuitive since those elements still take up space. display: none is the sneaky one because the element disappears visually but still occupies a DOM slot.

This is subtle. If you try to centralize the index on a parent:

…that --idx resolves right there on .parent. It grabs the parent’s own sibling index, locks it to that number, and every child inherits that single fixed value. Every child gets the same number. Almost certainly not what you want or expect.

The fix is simple — put the function on the elements that need it:

The CSSWG has discussed an inherits: declaration addition to @property that could theoretically fix this. If you haven’t used @property, it lets you define a custom property’s type, initial value, and inheritance behavior — way more control than a raw --variable. But the inherits: declaration idea is still in early CSSWG discussion, not baked into any spec draft. It could be years before it lands — or it might not land at all. Even with @property today, there’s no mechanism to say “don’t evaluate yet, wait for the child.” So for now, just apply directly.

Changing the DOM — i.e., adding, removing, reordering children — triggers style recalculation for affected siblings. The browser handles this during the cascade phase (before layout and paint), so it’s faster than the old approach of looping in JavaScript and stamping inline styles.

But there’s a real cost if you push it. Inserting an element at the beginning of a container with 10,000 children forces the engine to recalculate the sibling index for all 10,000 elements after it. For normal stuff — navigation, card grids, tab bars — you’ll never notice. For a live stock ticker or an infinite-scroll feed with thousands of nodes constantly churning, keep using JavaScript-managed indexes inside your virtualization window. These functions are fast. They’re not zero-cost.

As of writing, Chrome/Edge 138 shipped these functions in stable releases (June 2025), and Safari 26.2 followed. Firefox hasn’t shipped them in stable yet, but Mozilla’s spec position is positive and implementation work is actively underway — tracked under Bugzilla issue #1953973. Check caniuse for the latest before you ship.

Chrome and Safari together cover roughly 75–80% of global traffic. That’s a strong majority, but Firefox’s absence means you still need a fallback.

For shipping today, @supports is your friend:

Static fallback for Firefox. Mathematical layout for everyone else. Nobody gets a broken page.

This needs saying because it’s easy to get excited and forget: these functions are purely visual. They change how things look. They don’t change what things mean.

If you use sibling-index() math to visually reorder a list — via order or grid placement — a screen reader still reads the DOM in source order. Keyboard tab order follows the DOM, too. Visual layout and semantic structure will contradict each other, and that’s an accessibility failure.

For interactive components like data grids, radial menus, or custom listboxes that lean on tree-counting for layout, you still need JavaScript to sync ARIA attributes. aria-posinset and aria-setsize have no idea what CSS is calculating. If your CSS says “this is visually item 3 of 7” but ARIA says something different (or nothing), assistive technology users get a broken experience.

On the debugging side, recent versions of Chrome DevTools let you inspect computed sibling-index() and sibling-count() values directly in the Elements panel, which helps when the math isn’t doing what you expect.

The current spec only counts all element siblings. But the CSSWG has documented a planned extension in issue #9572: an of argument, matching what :nth-child() already supports.

Something like sibling-index(of .active) would let you count only siblings matching a specific selector. An element that’s the eighth child overall but the third .active child would return 3. For dynamic UIs where you’re filtering or toggling visibility, that would keep the index sequential without requiring DOM manipulation.

There’s also been CSSWG discussion around children-count() and descendant-count() functions — the first would tell you how many children an element has (useful for parent-driven layouts), the second would count all descendants recursively. Both are still at the proposal stage, but they’d round out the tree-counting story: sibling-index() and sibling-count() give you the horizontal view (where am I among my peers?), while children-count() and descendant-count() would give you the vertical view (what’s below me?).

That feeling I mentioned at the top — writing ten :nth-child() rules for a staggered animation and wondering if you’re missing something obvious? You weren’t. The obvious thing just didn’t exist yet.

#9473. A Famous Case of Shared Eyewitness 'Memory'

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

In previous posts of the Forensic View, we have seen that eyewitness memory, while frequently convincing to jurors and the public, is frequently and sometimes fabulously unreliable. But what happens when our confidence in reported eyewitness information is essentially “wired in parallel,” shared among different people who may, with repetition, put their own stamps on the information?

In 1914, during the First World War, these processes resulted in strongly held beliefs that Russian troops were coming.

All histories of that terrible conflict discuss the importance of Russian military operations in Eastern Europe. The hardships and horrifying casualty counts of that very harsh campaign are well attested.

But none of that happened in Scotland, where tens of thousands of entirely imaginary Russians were firmly believed to have turned up anyway.

The whole mess seems to have started on August 27th, 1914, when there was a long delay in the railway service linking London and Liverpool. Somebody, perhaps in an ill-advised attempt to boost morale, explained to somebody else that this was due to the diversion of trains which were transporting thousands of Russian troops, who had landed in Scotland, to reinforce the Western Front.

Word spread. These Russians’ route was allegedly very specific; they had crossed the Arctic Sea to Norway, then traveled by steamship to Aberdeen, and from there were being carried by special troop trains to the Channel ports.

Now, prior frameworks for understanding strongly influence our ability to remember and interpret information (Bransford & Johnson, 1973), even when those frameworks are completely incorrect, and the resulting memories and interpretations are therefore complete rubbish (Sharps, 2024; Sharps & Price-Sharps, 2026). However, when such frameworks, accurate or not, are filled with plausible feature-intensive detail, people may be increasingly inclined to believe them (Sharps, 2022, 2024); and the specificity of these peripatetic Russians’ itineraries helped to convince people of their absolute reality.

Additional details followed. Witnesses had supposedly seen Russians stamping snow off their boots at railway stations (Pennell, 2015). Makes sense—Russia has a lot of snow. Granted, how those troops managed to maintain that snow on their boots all the way to Edinburgh in August is quite a mystery (Tuchman, 1962); but since the story included the very specific detail of an imaginary railway porter who had swept up the imaginary snow, who was going to argue with this imaginary account?

Very reliable people had supposedly seen these Russians. An Oxford professor knew a colleague who’d been summoned as a Russian translator, and a Scots army officer had seen their big fur caps and, believe it or not, their bows and arrows. Why these Russian troops lacked modern weapons remains unexplained, but with enough popular momentum behind the story, people believed it anyway. The people of the time were under the extraordinary stress of horrible new types of warfare that produced casualty rates virtually beyond comprehension for that day—and it has been shown that when people are under stress, they are more likely to ignore evidentiary flaws in accounts (Sharps et al., 2013; Sharps, 2024).

Evidently, this psychological effect extended to snow in August and 20th-century Russian infantrymen armed like Robin Hood.

A Scots landowner personally reported 125,000 Russians marching across his property (Tuchman, 1962), which seems a bit low when 500,000 imaginary Russians were originally reported; but gradually these imaginary numbers dropped down to an equally imaginary 70,000 or 80,000, which presumably made people feel more confident about the realism of the whole imaginary business.

Some actual history became involved in this mess, as well. The naval battle of Heligoland Bight, which had nothing whatsoever to do with Russians, was explained as some form of weird diversion to cover the sea transport of these imaginary forces to Belgium (Tuchman, 1962). On the continent, people waited en masse in Paris to welcome their Cossack defenders. The Germans became concerned as well (Tuchman, 1962). Contemporary reports held that the Kaiser and his senior staff had left France from fear of the “250,000” Russian troops believed to be in the field there, and the German Army was reported to have detached two sorely needed divisions to repel this imaginary invasion from the Steppes.

Readers today may find this account mildly amusing, but essentially irrelevant to our modern lives. The First World War seems lost in remote antiquity, with the Red Baron, perhaps better known today for pizza than for aerial victories, flying about in a powered box-kite, and antique cannons being dragged around mud-soaked battlefields by teams of panicked horses. The whole thing may seem as remote to modern people as Crecy or Agincourt.

But if you were able to examine the brain of a person in 1914, you would find no substantive difference between that brain and the one in the head of any modern Internet-ridden person today. The effects of inaccurate prior frameworks, of stress-related reduction in critical thinking, and of the uncritical sharing of purported eyewitness accounts would be psychologically the same in the worlds of 1914 and 2026.

However, there would be an important exception today, based on our technology rather than our psychology. Unlike the word-of-mouth campaigns that spread false rumors in clubs and at railway stations in 1914, we of 2026 have the internet to spread false rumors worldwide at electronic speeds, either by mistake or by design on the part of people who have something to gain. We also have AI-generated imagery so advanced that its products are virtually impossible for most of us to tell from reality.

The remote and imaginary reports of Russians in Scotland in 1914 are more than a quaint episode in the history of eyewitness memory. They form a significant warning for those of us in the modern age of technology. Today, more than in any previous era, we must be very careful in our assessment of evidence, eyewitness, visual, and otherwise, and very aware of how the principles governing our psychology may influence that assessment.

Bransford, J. D., and Johnson, M. K. 1973. Considerations of Some Problems of Comprehension. In W. G. Chase (Ed.), Visual Information Processing. Orlando, FL: Academic Press.

Pennell, C. 2015. Believing the Unbelievable: The Myth of the Russians with 'Snow On Their Boots' in the United Kingdom, 1914. Cultural and Social History, 11, 69-87.

Sharps, M.J. 2022. Processing Under Pressure: Stress, Memory, and Decision-Making in Law Enforcement (3rd ed.). Park City, Utah: Blue 360 Media.

Sharps, M.J. 2024. The Forensic View: Investigative Psychology, Law Enforcement, Space Aliens, Exploration, and the Nature of Madness. Las Vegas: Amazon.

Sharps, M.J., Herrera, M.R., and Price‐Sharps, J.L. 2013. Situationally Equivocal Eyewitness Evidence and the Violence of Crimes. Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling, 10, DOI: 10.1002/jip.1398

Sharps, M.J., & Price-Sharps, J.L. 2026. Dissociation and Belief: The Psychology of Why Things Go Horribly Wrong, and What To Do About It. Las Vegas: Amazon.

Tuchman, B.W. 1962. The Guns of August. New York: Ballantine.

#9472. Dallas Art Fair scores new venue at football training facility

The field at Armstrong Fieldhouse, Southern Methodist University Photo courtesy of SMU, Eric Clement

The Dallas Art Fair will move to a new venue for the first time in its nearly two-decade history, relocating from downtown Dallas to an American football training facility on the campus of Southern Methodist University (SMU) for its 2027 edition. The fair, one of the leading independent commercial art fairs in the US, will take place 15-18 April at the university’s Armstrong Fieldhouse—an indoor training facility for SMU’s football team.

The move will give the fair more room to accommodate galleries and improve visitor experience, says fair director Kelly Cornell, while offering a fresh setting for an event that has outgrown its longtime home. “FIG has been an excellent home for us for the past 18 years, but it's also had its limitations in the sizing and amount of booths—those nitty-gritty details of producing a fair have been challenging,” Cornell says.

Since its inaugural edition in 2009, the Dallas Art Fair has occupied the Fashion Industry Gallery (FIG), a wholesale fashion market venue in downtown Dallas. FIG is owned by the local real-estate developer John Sughrue, who co-founded the fair with the curator Chris Byrne; Byrne left the organisation in 2017.

Earlier this year, FIG announced that it had extended its lease on the building until 2033, and local media reported that the fair would continue to be held there. Cornell says the organisation had been searching for a suitable alternative for nearly a decade, and that plans to relocate in 2027 came together quite quickly.

The Dallas Art Fair at its former home at FIG (Fashion Industry Gallery) Courtesy Dallas Art Fair

The Armstrong Fieldhouse offers a more flexible layout than FIG, where fair exhibitors had been split across two floors with limited visibility between them. The new venue will bring everyone together on one level playing field—literally—with higher ceilings and fewer physical obstructions to work around.

The fair will need to cover the playing surface, but Cornell says she intends to retain the field goals. “It’s an easy blank slate that we can load one story in and out,” she says. “The logistics were excellent, and then it took getting the university support and buy-in.”

The fair first became interested in the fieldhouse three years ago, Cornell says. The ushering in of SMU’s president, Jay Hartzell, and provost, Rachel Davis Mersey, in recent years have helped bring the university on board to partner with the fair.

The private university, nicknamed Southern Millionaire’s University, has more than 12,000 students. It is located in University Park, around five miles north of downtown Dallas, and borders Highland Park, an affluent neighbourhood that is home to many of the city’s art collectors. Cornell says the fair’s new location will be walkable for many visitors, and the partnership with SMU could bring good relationships with both the university’s board and students having their first experiences with commercial art.

The fair does not intend to expand dramatically in exhibitor numbers for its 2027 edition. It typically presents around 90 galleries (with the total closer to 100 in the years before the pandemic), but the limitations of FIG left little scope for growth. Now, the new venue is expected to give participating galleries greater flexibility to create larger installations and more immersive presentations.

The move will also allow the fair to improve circulation and introduce an upscale dining option on site. Other planned upgrades include higher walls, improved lighting and infrastructure, and more space for hospitality and sponsors.

“The intention is to continue to increase the quality of the fair and provide better space for our galleries,” Cornell says. “Twelve-foot walls, nicer infrastructure and lighting, being able to provide more hospitality and sponsor spaces within the footprint—the goal is to be the best fair of our size in the world.”

For the first time, it will share the stage with the smaller boutique fair Dallas Invitational

The Texas fair has a record of resilience, largely shielded from economic dips that affected the US at large, but this year’s edition will be the art market's first major test since President Trump's new tariffs

As demand for art in Dallas and the rest of Texas heats up, dealers are eager to get a foothold in the Lone Star State—including at the new-ish Dallas Invitational satellite fair

#9470. Why We Delay Important Decisions

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I’m sure you can relate to putting off an important decision until next week, then the week after that, and then the week after that. Maybe you need to decide where you would like to relocate, choose a healthcare provider, or determine whether to move forward with an important medical procedure. You know the decision needs your attention, but you keep finding reasons to wait.

Most of us may think of procrastination as putting things off because we are busy or lack motivation. However, what if we are not avoiding the task itself, but the uncertainty that comes with making a decision? Oftentimes, the most difficult part is not knowing what to do, but accepting that we cannot predict how things will turn out.

Experts argue that one reason this happens is negative reinforcement. When avoiding something uncomfortable brings relief, our brains will likely desire to avoid it again. Consider, for example, when a deadline gets pushed back. In the moment, you may feel better knowing you have more time to complete the task at hand, even though you know that the work still needs to get done. Delaying an important decision can have the same effect. We may receive temporary relief, however the decision still remains unresolved.

In my work with people facing difficult life decisions, I have seen how the desire to avoid making the wrong choice can become a significant barrier. People may spend considerable time weighing possibilities, seeking reassurance, and revisiting the same concerns.

Another reason important decisions can be difficult to make is that we want to make the best possible choice. Experts describe this tendency as maximizing. It involves searching for the best available option, rather than choosing one that meets our needs and priorities. Wanting to make a good decision is reasonable, but constantly searching for something better can make it harder to settle on an option.

Let's think about someone deciding whether to relocate for a new job. The opportunity they are considering may offer better pay and career growth, however accepting it could mean leaving family, familiar surroundings, and comfort. They may continue comparing options and questioning whether another opportunity would have been better, even after obtaining enough information to inform their decision.

Recent research offers some insight into this pattern. For instance, in a 2024 study, researchers examined how people with maximizing tendencies estimate the time they spend making decisions. Results showed that "maximizers" tended to underestimate how much time they spent comparing and reconsidering their options. They likely don't realize they are making decision-making harder not easier for themselves.

Making a decision becomes even more challenging when we are faced with too many options to select from. For instance, someone who has decided to undergo a medical procedure, but must choose how to pay for it, has to decide on using a credit card, applying for a medical credit line, choosing an in-house payment plan, or financing through a third-party company, which adds another decision to an already important one.

One emerging example in the healthcare industry is "first-look financing." An article by Cherry describes how this concept introduces one preferred financing option first while keeping other options available. This approach reflects choice architecture, which examines how the presentation of choices can influence people's decisions.

For example, after a patient agrees to move forward with a medical procedure, the clinic might first explain its preferred third-party financing option, including the monthly payment and application process. If the patient is not comfortable with that option, the provider can then discuss other options, such as an in-house payment plan or using a credit card.

Here are a few ways to make important decisions feel more manageable:

Putting off important decisions is something many of us experience, especially when we are uncertain about what may happen next. Avoiding a decision can make us feel better temporarily, but it does not necessarily make the situation easier. Ultimately, we do not have to find the perfect option or know exactly how everything will turn out before moving forward. Sometimes, making a good-enough decision and taking one small step at a time is what can help us move past the uncertainty.

Cheek, N. N., & Schwartz, B. (2016). On the meaning and measurement of maximization. Judgment and Decision Making, 11(2), 126–146. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500007257

Huang and Li (2024). “How Maximizers Estimate Their Decision Time: The Mediating Effect of Memory Reduction.” Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 37(3).

#9469. Four Levels Of Customer Understanding

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Many companies think they know fairly well what their users want and need, and how they make their decisions. Yet most of the time these are merely big assumptions and big hunches — with little real evidence to support them. In practice, obvious reasons might be true, but they rarely paint the full picture.

To understand our customers, we must triangulate across four levels of customer understanding by Hannah Shamji. It’s a useful way to think about the underlying reasons for user behavior, hidden motivations, and the complex layers of messy and noisy reality that are often overlooked. Let’s see how it works.

To learn about customers, it might seem reasonable to ask people what they think and draw conclusions from it. But it’s rarely an effective way to get actionable answers. In fact, as it turns out, what people think, feel, say, and do are often very different things.

As Erika Hall wrote, asking a question directly is the worst way to get a true and useful answer to that question. We don’t always understand or are aware of our true motivations. We often apply our own context and interpretations to questions.

We also exaggerate (a lot!). We focus on edge cases and unrealistic scenarios, and we favor short-term goals over long-term goals. So if users say that they absolutely need to compare products in a table, it doesn’t mean that they couldn’t get to their underlying goal without it.

Just to indicate how tricky listening to words alone is: even little nuances in words chosen matter. In practice, users are rarely precise in expressing their thoughts, and a good example is the distinction between possible, plausible, and probable, as discovered by Thomas D’hooge.

A study on Dutch verbal probability terms shows how unreliable the choice of words is. While extreme words have some agreement, terms like “possible,” “maybe,” “uncertain,” or “likely” lead to a wide spread of interpretations. So we shouldn’t rely on what people say, but rather try to go deeper.

To get a more realistic and less biased view of customers’ needs, we need to understand a broader picture across 4 levels:

Personally, I wouldn’t recommend NPS (alternative). It’s worth noting that different levels might reveal conflicting or contradictory data. To get a better understanding, we need to triangulate and reconcile data with mixed-method research.

Emotions are always difficult to capture, but they are easier to spot once you observe people doing what they need to do without external influence or interruptions. The ability to positively impact users grows by moving from sympathy to empathy or even compassion, as articulated by Sarah Gibbons.

In the past, I was using “speak-aloud” protocol and asked users to walk me through their thought process as they were completing tasks. But it actually turns out to be quite disruptive. Because people are focused on speaking at the same time while solving a task, many emotions remain hidden or obscured by their language.

So, when conducting usability testing, I don’t ask users to speak through their experience. Instead, I observe where they tap or hover with the mouse, where their mouse circles without an action, where they scroll, and how long. Eventually, when a user confirms that they are done or that they are stuck, I ask questions.

The Emotion Wheel (website) by Geoffrey Roberts is a helpful little tool for better describing a range of emotions during user interviews or design sessions. It certainly needs refinement for product design needs, but it helps us get more precise about the sentiment customers or colleagues might be experiencing, moving beyond just “good” or “bad”.

One helpful trick is to use mirroring — repeating what a user has said, or ask the same question twice, just paraphrasing it. Or navigating the emotions wheel (see above) to better capture and understand the emotion.

These strategies help uncover some of the issues that perhaps didn’t come up in the first answer. That’s also when a user tends to add more useful context and details as they explain their confusion.

I think that Alin brings up a very strong argument, and personally, I find it difficult to disagree with. However, I do see user’s emotional response as a signal of how well the product is working for them. How engaged or detached they are in their journey, how they react to aesthetics, how confused or confident they are.

Ultimately, these are signals. To make a difference, we must go beyond emotions and explore what people actually do. Usually, this means relentlessly observing, diagnosing, and focusing on underlying user needs.

Instead of asking, we need to observe. Usually, I focus on small things that make or break an experience. I see where users lose time, repeat actions, hover without clicking, or click and then go back. Pay attention to subtle cues like scratching their neck, raising eyebrows, or expressions of worry, joy, or confusion.

Many companies talk about “validation” through user testing, but often that means simply confirming existing assumptions. But we should instead diagnose existing behavior without preconceived notions or affiliations. We don’t validate — we actually research instead.

That research means not just understanding customers’ real motivations, but also risks, doubts, concerns, worries, and perhaps even harms.

The only way to get there is by building a sincere, honest, and trustworthy relationship — one that feels right and resonates deeply. When customers truly care and want to help, getting to a real understanding becomes much, much easier.

We don’t need expensive tools to uncover user needs. David Travis provides a fantastic overview of helpful strategies to do just that. Here are some initiatives to spread the word about real user’s struggles or gain a deeper understanding of user needs:

The core idea here is that you don’t need extensive and expensive tools to uncover user needs. You need to create spaces where customers’ struggles can be exposed and make these struggles visible across the entire company.

It can be short video clips of user sessions or a monthly newsletter with what we learned this month. Making these pain points visible can rally everyone from marketing to engineering to keep users’ struggles at the back of their minds.

To make an impact, we must go way beyond user feedback. It’s never enough to listen to surveys — we must observe customers’ actual behaviors and build relationships to truly understand their goals and their motivations.

And most importantly, we need to understand what questions we actually want to have answered. Not what “validation” we need to move on with the project, but what we don’t know and what we need to research.

Without it, everything else is merely hunches and assumptions — and often wrong and expensive ones.

#9468. Top 10 Issues to Consider for Polyamorous Parents

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

The popularity of divorce and nonmarital childbirth means that many people who already have children later form romantic relationships with other adults. Polyamorists and other nonmonogamous parents also form new romantic relationships. All of that means that parents need to figure out how their partners will interact with their children.

The following list is inspired by Polyam Parenting founder Jen Gerardy’s work on polyamorous parenting. A Holistic Family Consultant, breastfeeding advisor, and mediator, Gerardy helps parents juggle the commitments and emotional work of raising children in non-monogamous families. Below I condense Gerardy’s work and divide it into three sections:

1. Titles: What will we call each other? What will the child call each of us? Who gets to decide? Many polyamorous families often use the adults’ first names until otherwise noted. If the child(ren) want to call the adults something else, the kids usually create the name or nickname.

2. Affection: How are we going to express affection in front of the child? How do we show affection to the child, and how are they allowed to show affection to adults? For example, many parents prefer to allow their children to choose if they want to hug an adult or not, though some older adults can get very upset when a child refuses to hug them. How will the polycule handle it if their child does not want to hug Great Auntie Sue?

3. Time: How much time will we spend together with the child? How much time will members of the polycule spend with each other, apart from the child? Who will spend solo time with the child, and under what circumstances? Who is responsible for the child at various times? Who gets free time from parental responsibilities?

4. Daily care: How will we manage the feeding, transit, supervision, dressing, hygiene, and discipline of the children? How will the adults navigate it if someone feeds the child too much sugar or fails to make them brush their teeth? Who is responsible for overseeing the children’s daily well-being?

5. Space or housing: Who lives where, and what are the boundaries of the children’s space? What kind of space is dedicated to the adults? Who is responsible for financing, cleaning, organizing, and furnishing it? Who has their own space and who has to share? Is a partner moving into the child’s existing home? Is the child moving in with a partner? Do people live separately but spend quite a bit of time in each other’s environments? What boundaries shape the kids’ access to space?

6. Behavior: How do we behave towards each other as parents? How do we behave towards the kids? Who is responsible for the kids’ behavior? Who has the authority to enforce consequences for misbehavior?

7. Money: Who pays for the kids to go to college? Who buys their clothes, food, and housing? Who will pay for medical bills or orthodontia? How will the adults work out collaborative and/or separate money for themselves and the children?

8. Milestones: Who is invited to attend parties, birthdays, retirement events, weddings, funerals, holiday meals, and all the other holidays or events? What kinds of gifts do we give each other, and the kids? How do we present each other to others? What if some people are out as polyamorous but others are closeted?

9. Official recognition: Who is the legal representative of the children? Who can make medical and/or educational decisions? How many people can sign up to pick them up from school, and under what circumstances? Who can act as an emergency contact?

10. If the adults break up: Who is allowed to maintain contact with the children after the adults break up, and how can they do so? What circumstances do people need to retain contact with the kids and other adults in the polycule, and when do they know to cut contact with their exes? If the adults cut contact, will the children also be required to cut contact? Who has financial obligations to the children? Who has financial obligations to the other adults for raising the children (alimony)? Who has custody of the children, who is allowed visitation, and who gets to decide?

Polycules that are adding new partners to existing children’s lives or planning to have children together must consider many things. As with so many things connected to nonmonogamy, communication turns out to be a crucial ingredient when creating family boundaries. Gerardy believes that polyamorous people can have close relationships with their children and partners as long as they balance their time and energy.

“Polyamory and parenting requires self-reflection, strong boundaries, clear communication, and healthy community, but it pays dividends in fulfilling relationships for you and your kids. The first and most important step any parent, future parent, or someone dating a parent can take is to really be clear about what you need and what works for you. Do you need a lot of quiet time, or do you prefer to be surrounded by bustle? Do you want partners to be supports for the challenges of daily life, or a break from the mundane? What is important in your life beyond the roles of parent and partner? The more honestly you approach your own needs and wants, the more openly you can collaborate with potential partners on their role in your children's lives.”

Obviously, there are more than 10 issues for any parent to explore, and that is true here as well. Discussing these top 10 issues with your partners, no matter what kind of blended family you create, can help polycules and other blended families negotiate clear boundaries and expectations with adults and kids. It can help people decide if and when they want to co-parent with others, and where they might disagree on current or future issues. Exploring these issues before having children, or as early in a dating relationship as possible, can help alleviate future stress.

Gerardy, Jen. (2026). The Child Rearing Smorgasboard. https://www.polyamparenting.com/tools/the-child-rearing-smorgasbord

#9467. New York’s Socrates Sculpture Park rebuilds for resilience and expands

The park’s inaugural show in 1986 included a towering Mark di Suvero work Courtesy Socrates Sculpture Park

When Superstorm Sandy hit New York City in 2012, Socrates Sculpture Park, located on the Queens riverfront, disappeared underwater. With a four-foot rise in sea level, water streamed from the park into the surrounding area, which was at that time comprised mostly of factories and the neighbouring Noguchi Museum.

Fourteen years later, the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation broke ground last month on the park’s seawall reconstruction. This work, which has been unfolding at riverfront parks across the city with funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, necessitates that much of Socrates’s five-acre campus remain closed until its completion next spring.

A former landfill and illegal dumping ground turned green space that supports artists in the production and presentation of public art, Socrates’s founding is described by executive director Shaun Leonardo as “a radical act of land transformation”. In this same spirit, Socrates will unveil on 31 October—during its annual Halloween Harvest Festival—the transformation of a largely abandoned storage area on the park’s southern edge into a revitalised landscape featuring a long-term installation of three monumental sculptures by the park’s founding artist Mark di Suvero.

Called The Point, this one-acre expansion, Leonardo says, is an opportunity to “connect Socrates’s future to its founding story” on the occasion of its 40th anniversary. Though this parcel has historically been a maintenance and storage location to support the creation and installation of work by Socrates artists—including Di Suvero who built many of his towering sculptures at the park in the 1980s and 90s—it has steadily grown dormant. Now, at age 93, he primarily lives on the West Coast, but the three soon-to-be-unveiled sculptures have lived on-site since their creation (1995 for the earliest, 2017 for the most recent). While they are comprised of steel I-beams, like much of his work, these sculptures are dynamic and meant to be engaged with: two include a swing; one of those also features a spinning titanium element.

Di Suvero’s “work feels like drawing in space and, through that lens, you really start to see how much he thought about it interacting in its environment”, Leonardo says.

A view of Socrates Sculpture Park in 2020 with Jeffrey Gibson's Because Once You Enter My House It Becomes Our House in the foreground Courtesy of KMDeco Creative Solutions

Established in 1986 by a coalition of artists and community members, Socrates grew out of Di Suvero’s nearby studio located in a defunct brick warehouse. Having brought in a team to help install his works, he also shared his space with other sculptors and gave them access to his tools. Together, they looked at the neighbouring landfill and “saw an opportunity again to extend the work they were doing in the studio into a space to develop works in public view, and in deep connection with the neighbourhood,” Leonardo says.

With the establishment of a workforce development programme—whereby residents of the nearby Astoria Houses public housing complex were hired to both clear the land and help artists fabricate their projects—Socrates revitalised the landscape while creating, as Leonardo puts it, an “economic engine of an opportunity for individuals to build up a skill set not only in horticulture, but in fabrication, maintenance, community engagement and public event production, knowing that they could leave from Socrates to full employment elsewhere”. Though the programme had fallen dormant since the Covid-19 pandemic, Leonardo relaunched it this year with a pilot edition supported by the Ford Foundation and Urban Upbound.

The factories that formerly populated the neighbourhood have in recent years been replaced by residential high-rises that are just as vulnerable to the next storm as the park is, if not more so. “What’s unique about erosion of a landfill, as opposed to a natural landscape,” Leonardo says, is that “not only has the rock shoreline disappeared, but the coast is caving in as well because of what is being eroded from underneath.”

“We have taken it upon ourselves to think about our work as it relates to climate resilience as a responsibility to both people and place,” he adds. “Much of our landscaping system has been strategic in terms of not only soil rehabilitation but also flood mitigation and providing a better barrier to the neighbourhood.” That has included, for example, cultivating native plants and restoring the habitat for monarch butterflies along their migration route.

“In order for the community to thrive,” Leonardo says, “the art has to serve an additional purpose of giving to that community and being in reciprocal relationship with the land.”

New York’s outdoor art landscape is full of surprises this season, from mounds of oysters on Governors Island and bathing birds near City Hall to a towering corn cob on the High Line and a gargantuan teddy bear in Queens

A new work by the artist will be on offer for the first time at Socrates Sculpture Park’s annual benefit, with proceeds going to the park.

The year-long programme Monuments Now at Socrates Sculpture Park in Queens aims to evaluate ideas around public art
