#9466. The Thing Your Friends Don’t Tell You About Being Single

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Time on your own can teach you steadiness, awareness, and self-compassion, so you bring your whole self into your next relationship.

I used to hear the phrase “you need to be single to work on yourself” and find it almost offensive, as if someone were saying I was too damaged or too complicated to be loved until I fixed myself.

Over time, I realized that wasn’t what people meant.

Being single isn’t about becoming more worthy of love.

Being single isn’t about becoming more worthy of love. It’s about finally having enough space to understand yourself without another person’s emotions, habits, and reactions constantly shaping the environment around you.

Because relationships don’t just connect two people. They connect two nervous systems.

The person you are closest to influences how you feel, how you respond, and how quickly you return to calm. Their presence can give you perspective, reduce uncertainty, or make difficult moments feel easier.

That comfort is real, but comfort and growth are not always the same thing.

Sometimes what feels like healing is actually relief. You feel better because someone else is helping you feel okay again, but you haven’t necessarily learned how to create that stability within yourself.

There is nothing wrong with needing connection. Humans are wired for it. The problem comes when we never learn the difference between being supported by someone and needing someone to feel whole.

Growth happens when you discover you can sit with discomfort and still find your footing.

Growth happens when you discover you can sit with discomfort and still find your footing. When you can experience fear, uncertainty, or sadness without immediately needing another person to make those feelings disappear.

That is one of the hardest things to learn while staying inside the same patterns you are trying to change.

Two people rarely grow at the same pace or in the same direction. One person starts setting boundaries while the other is used to having access. Someone begins to pause before reacting while the other is still waiting for the old response. As one person changes, the relationship has to decide whether it can change with them.

Sometimes it can, and sometimes it can’t. That is where solitude can become powerful.

Solitude is not about proving you can live without anyone…The purpose of that space is to hear yourself clearly.

Solitude is not about proving you can live without anyone. Independence is not the goal. The purpose of that space is to hear yourself clearly and understand what belongs to you before bringing that awareness back into connection with someone else.

You start noticing your own reactions more clearly. Old wounds become easier to recognize. You learn to separate what comes from within you from what was shaped by the dynamic you were in.

The advice to “be single for a while” isn’t a punishment.

It is an invitation to stop abandoning yourself while trying to build a life with someone else.

Because change is harder when you are still surrounded by the exact dynamics that shaped the patterns you are trying to break.

Being alone gives you the chance to learn that you can regulate your own emotions and make decisions from clarity instead of fear.

It is not impossible, but it does require more awareness, effort, and intention.

Being alone gives you the chance to learn that you can regulate your own emotions and make decisions from clarity instead of fear. It also gives you space to build a secure relationship with yourself, without relying on someone else to create that stability for you.

Then, when you do enter a relationship again, you’re not looking for someone to complete what is missing.

You are bringing a whole person into the room.

#9465. 3 Steps to De-Catastrophize Your Anxious Thoughts

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

People with anxiety often come to therapy complaining of a specific and extreme form of worrying. They ask questions like:

If your mind also plays a reel of worst-case scenarios every time your anxiety rises, you might be engaging in catastrophizing. Catastrophic thinking is distorted perception and cognition.

Typically, when a person catastrophizes, they blow things out of proportion and feel irrationally threatened by current, past, or imaginary situations. If you tend to catastrophize, here are three steps to de-escalate your thought processes.

Catastrophizing can quickly lead you down a dark thought spiral. The best thing to do: Immediately bring yourself back to the present.

Research published in Acta Psychologica suggests that mindfulness, both in the moment and as a personality trait, shows great promise as a combatant to anxiety and catastrophizing. Training and practicing mindfulness can give your emotion regulation faculties a much-needed boost.

Another practice that can help someone who struggles with catastrophizing is breathwork. Research shows that deep breathing — or diaphragmatic breathing — relieves anxiety by lowering heart rate and blood pressure. Focusing on your breath grounds you in the present and therefore acts as a buffer between you and your catastrophic thoughts.

Small worries accumulate and turn into catastrophic thinking. Research explains that setting aside and scheduling a block of time solely for worrying is a simple but effective stress-management technique.

If you have anxious or catastrophic thoughts during an important moment, defer them to your ‘worry time’ and focus on the present moment. It can also help you become aware of and address your anxieties.

Since catastrophizing is a cognitive distortion or, simply put, a malfunctioning thought process, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is recommended most often when it comes to addressing catastrophic thinking.

Research shows CBT is effective against catastrophizing; it is based on awareness. Under CBT, the person struggling with catastrophizing is made aware of the dysfunction in emotion regulation and thought processes and is given exercises tailored to dismantle irrational thinking.

Often, the best antidote to catastrophic thinking is to talk to someone who can offer an objective perspective, like a therapist or counselor.

As with other distorted thought processes, catastrophizing flourishes in isolation. The first thing anyone should do when they can’t control their own disturbing thoughts is to say them out loud, preferably to a loved one or a medical professional.

#9464. Your Prototype Is Not Being Honest With Your Users (And Here’s How To Fix It)

Eric is a Creative Technologist at ProtoPie, where he pushes the boundaries of no-code prototyping. With a background in FinTech UX design, he brings firsthand … More about Eric ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at ProtoPie who help users turn their ideas into highly interactive animations and prototypes for mobile, desktop, web, and IoT. Thank you!

There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness.

In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance users are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

Preview both fields: username shows text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

Add a new scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

Select Log In, add a Tap trigger, set response to Jump, target your dashboard scene, transition Slide in from right to left.

Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

At the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:

Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:

Move the Jump response inside this condition. Wrong credentials, empty fields, wrong format: none get through. Participants now have to actually log in. That single constraint changes the texture of every test session that follows.

Find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

This is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

This tutorial is part of the FinTech Prototyping with ProtoPie series on the ProtoPie blog. The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.

#9462. Why You Shouldn’t Take Anything Personally

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Don’t take anything personally. Easier said than done. This represents the second agreement in the bestselling book The Four Agreements written by Don Miguel Ruiz (1997). In it, he astutely states, "Even when a situation seems so personal, even if others insult you directly, it has nothing to do with you. What they say, what they do, and the opinions they give are according to the agreements they have in their own minds."

Despite this, we find ourselves allowing someone's criticism, disapproval, or lack of responsiveness to determine how we feel about ourselves. Our mood and confidence can instantly shift because of a perceived disapproving tone or sensing that we’re the cause of someone’s irritation or frustration. We may react irrationally, impulsively, and intensely based on someone’s reactions, and our perceptions and interpretations.

Taking things personally is often an automatic psychological response shaped by our insecurities, attachment experiences, learned beliefs, and fundamental desire and need to belong. Research suggests that perceived rejection can activate our sympathetic nervous system, helping explain why interpersonal slights can feel disproportionately painful (Eisenberger et al., 2003).

1. You do not like everyone; therefore, you cannot expect that everyone will like you.

Consider how many people you have encountered whom you did not particularly connect or resonate with. Sometimes we have negative feelings that get evoked solely by someone’s presence or mannerism, even if there isn’t any rational justification for it.

Our personal preferences are influenced by many factors such as another’s personality, values, expectations, etc. When we’re not readily accepted, or outwardly rejected, we assume and interpret it as evidence of our inadequacy or lack of worthiness.

Our brain’s tendency is to seek external approval and acceptance and gauge it as a valid measure of our worth. We’re taught this early on in our development and societal standards reinforce it. We frame it as: “If they think I have value, then I must. If they think I do not, then I must not.”

We do not learn that someone else’s preference or opinion is just that, and that our standards and opinion about ourselves matter most. You can reframe and consider that someone's preference for you doesn't determine your value, and you can be an incredible person, despite not being someone’s preferred person.

2. You cannot read minds. Your triggers, perceptions, judgments, and assumptions are all yours.

We frequently confuse our thoughts, feelings, and interpretations as absolute facts. If someone mistakenly doesn’t acknowledge us, we conclude that they don’t care about us and we’re not important enough to them. We also sometimes fail to own and take accountability for our own triggers and often get defensive, deflect, and blame to avoid facing our own fears and vulnerabilities.

In relationships, mind reading, personalization, catastrophizing, and other cognitive distortions can skew reality and be counterproductive and harmful (Beck, 2020). The inaccuracy is understandable given that our mind constructs explanations based on our past experiences, expectations, and emotional states.

To balance out your thinking, you can ask yourself: "What do I actually know, and what am I assuming? How else can I see this?" This is approaching the circumstance and person with overarching openness, curiosity, and expansiveness.

3. Criticism, aggression, and other harsh responses may reflect someone else's internal struggles.

Individuals can externalize their shame, frustration, insecurity, or unresolved emotional pain through hostility, defensiveness, or criticism. Psychodynamic theory describes projection as a defense mechanism through which individuals attribute aspects of their internal experience to others (Bailey & Pico 2023).

For example, a highly insecure person may be especially critical toward others. To distinguish whether a projection is being enacted, you can consider their delivery, intensity, or emotional reaction.

4. Negative energy is to be observed, not absorbed.

Imagine someone is speaking to you impatiently and with irritability. Within seconds, your chest tightens, your heart rate accelerates, your thoughts spiral, and you feel compelled to relent to protect yourself or actively defend yourself. Their emotional state has comingled and become yours.

Research on emotional contagion suggests that people can influence one another's emotional experiences, sometimes without conscious awareness (Wang, 2024). Self-awareness, self-regulation, and self-compassion don't require emotional absorption.

You can connect with and offer empathy for someone else’s reaction and experiences without absorbing and taking on their negative energy. It requires thoughtfully and mindfully deciphering what is theirs and what is yours, and how you choose to react to it.

5. Someone's negative mood is not automatically about you.

You may encounter distance, irritability enacted by a harsh tone or body language. Your immediate thought might be, "What did I do?" We often personalize others’ behavior, as connected to something we said or did, without evidence to support it.

Their mood can be reflective of their disappointment, fatigue, hormones, stress, or concerns that can be entirely unrelated to you. Before jumping to conclusions, approach with curiosity and consider asking, "I wonder if something’s going on for you. Is everything okay?" You can choose to approach with compassion and be attuned to someone's emotions without automatically assuming you're responsible for them.

Rejection can be particularly painful because belonging is a fundamental psychological need. Experiencing rejection can contribute to negative self-confidence, social anxiety, and the ability to sustain healthy trusting friendships and intimate relationships.

When someone rejects us, we often transform a specific experience into a more global conclusion. We make inferences such as “They didn’t choose me" becomes "I'm not good enough." Even though intellectually we know that rejection can reflect differing needs, incompatibility, timing, or circumstances beyond what we can control, we tend to personalize and generalize it.

You can remind yourself that your worth isn't determined by whether someone recognizes, attunes to, appreciates, or chooses you. You can’t avoid rejection, but you can strengthen your self-respect and self-compassion based on how you respond to it.

7. People's reactions provide you with vital information.

You can learn a lot from observing others’ reactions. It can give you a glimpse of their expectations, perspective, judgments, and emotional state. Emotional maturity involves vulnerability in noticing and acknowledging each person’s contribution, taking accountability, and repairing and healing when appropriate.

In order to accomplish this, you can identify if there is a difference of opinion, a divergent way of seeing circumstances, or an altered way of behaving based on differing core values. The goal is to evaluate, validate and reach mutual understanding so that future interactions can be healthier and more satisfying.

8. Proactively protect your emotional energy.

We can spend hours self-doubting, replaying conversations, anticipating rejection, questioning ourselves, or trying to change someone else's opinion of us. This rumination or perseveration spirals into thoughts about the thoughts, feelings about the feelings, thoughts about the feelings, and feelings about the thoughts. The emotional cost is exhaustion, exasperation, and typically extends beyond the original interaction.

Learning to notice, acknowledge, and interrupt your thoughts allows you to redirect your attention, even though your mind wants desperately to problem-solve. You could more readily focus on what you can directly influence, such as your interpretations, boundaries, responses, and choices.

The greatest emotional freedom comes when you no longer require other people to behave differently to feel secure within yourself. You recognize that you have choices regarding the way you respond.

You can recognize that you can be impacted by someone’s behavior without it defining you or automatically driving your behavior.

It can be challenging to notice parts of yourself that you would rather avoid or rid yourself of. Your activation, which can manifest itself as aggression, distancing, or in other ways, is about you. No one triggers you; you get triggered. Recognizing that can change not only how you experience others, but how you experience yourself.

Here is a Stop Taking Things Personally Guided Meditation to help you cultivate emotional freedom and inner peace.

Bailey, R., & Pico, J. (2023). Defense mechanisms. In StatPearls. Saint Petersburg, FL: StatPearls Publishing. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559106/.

Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). NY: Guilford Press.

Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., & Williams, K. D. (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science, 302(5643), 290–292. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1089134.

Ruiz, D. M. (1997). The four agreements: A practical guide to personal freedom. San Rafael, CA: Amber-Allen Publishing.

Wang, D., Liu, C., & Chen, W. (2024). The role of self-representation in emotional contagion. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 18, Article 1361368. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2024.1361368.

#9461. Algorithmic Theming Engines: Building Self-Correcting Color Systems With `contrast-color()`

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The HTTP Archive Web Almanac has been tracking color contrast failures for years. The numbers have barely moved. After half a decade of design system tooling, accessibility linters, and entire JavaScript libraries dedicated to computing readable text colors, 70% of websites still fail basic WCAG contrast checks in 2025. The WebAIM Million paints an even grimmer picture — 83.9% of homepages flagged for low contrast text in 2026, up from 79.1% in 2025. The rate improves by maybe a few percentage points per year on one benchmark and actually gets worse on another. That’s not progress — that’s proof that relying on runtime JavaScript for something this fundamental doesn’t scale across the open web. We didn’t need better libraries. We’ve needed better CSS.

The contrast-color() function is that better CSS. One declaration. The browser runs the contrast math during style computation, before the page paints, and hands you the right text color. No library, no build step, no hydration flash.

Note: If you’ve seen it called color-contrast() in older articles and spec drafts — that name was changed, and the old syntax no longer works in any browser.

The Level 5 version is simple. You give it a color. It gives you back black or white, whichever has more contrast against your input.

Change --brand-color to neon green, text goes black. Change it to midnight navy, text goes white. Swap themes at runtime via JavaScript and the text adapts instantly — no event listeners, no recalculation.

A few things to know about the current version:

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

This function lives across two specifications. That’s unusual and worth understanding.

CSS Color Level 5 defines what browsers ship today. One color in, black or white out. The algorithm is deliberately marked “UA-defined”, meaning the browser decides what math to use internally. Right now, every engine uses WCAG 2.x relative luminance. But that “UA-defined” label isn’t accidental — it’s a planned escape hatch.

You’ll see APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) mentioned a lot in this context. APCA models how human eyes actually perceive contrast, factoring in font weight, spatial frequency, and ambient light — a genuine improvement over the WCAG 2.x formula. By not locking “use WCAG 2.x” into the Level 5 spec, browser vendors could swap to APCA later without breaking any existing code. If the spec had shipped with a wcag2() keyword as the default, every site using it would’ve been stuck on the old math permanently.

But APCA’s future is far less certain than the hype suggests. Adrian Roselli’s “WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026” lays out the current situation clearly: APCA was pulled from the WCAG 3 working draft in mid-2023 after failing to gain enough Working Group support. The WCAG 3 spec currently says the contrast algorithm is “yet to be determined,” and the standard itself may not be finalized until 2030 or later. Roselli also filed a Chromium issue in May 2024 asking for the “Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm” experiment flag to be removed from DevTools entirely, arguing that the implementation is outdated and risks misleading developers into thinking APCA is further along — or more official — than it actually is. That issue is still open.

None of this means APCA is dead. The research behind it is peer-reviewed and substantive, and its creator has noted that colors passing APCA guidelines greatly exceed WCAG 2 minimums in the vast majority of cases. But right now, there is no guarantee APCA will be the algorithm that replaces WCAG 2.x — and that uncertainty matters for contrast-color(). If a different algorithm wins out, or if WCAG 3 adopts something entirely new, the “UA-defined” label means browsers can adapt without breaking your code. It also means the Level 6 features — candidate color lists, target ratios, the tbd-fg/tbd-bg keywords — are all designed around an algorithm that may or may not materialize in its current form.

CSS Color Level 6 adds the extended syntax — candidate color lists and target contrast ratios:

The browser would evaluate each candidate left to right and pick the first that meets the 4.5:1 AA threshold. The tbd-fg and tbd-bg keywords indicate whether the base color is foreground or background, which matters for directional contrast models like APCA. This is all Working Draft territory — doubly so given APCA’s uncertain status. Use the Level 5 version for now.

This one’s in better shape than most new CSS features. All three major engines have shipped it in stable releases: Chrome 147 (April 2026), Firefox 146, and Safari 26.0. It reached Baseline Newly Available status in April 2026. Check caniuse for the full version matrix. All three engines pass the Web Platform Tests for contrast-color(), which means the edge cases (e.g., tie-breaking logic, color space conversion, syntax parsing) behave the same across browsers.

The raw global support percentage on caniuse looks low, but that mostly reflects enterprise browsers and people who never update. If you’re reading this, your browser almost certainly supports it already.

Progressive enhancement is straightforward using @supports:

Older browsers get white text with a dark shadow for legibility. Supporting browsers get the native calculation. Nobody sees broken text.

One thing to watch for: automated accessibility scanners (Lighthouse, Axe, etc.) can’t evaluate text-shadow. They only look at the computed color against background-color. So the fallback will still get flagged as a contrast failure in CI/CD pipelines, even if the shadow makes the text perfectly legible to human eyes. If your team runs automated a11y checks, you may need to allowlist that specific rule or add a comment explaining why the flag is a false positive.

This can trip people up: “I used the contrast function, so my site passes accessibility checks now, right?”

Mathematically? Usually yes. There is a persistent myth that for certain “mid-tone” backgrounds, both black and white fail the standard WCAG 4.5:1 AA ratio. That’s mathematically false. Under the WCAG 2.x relative luminance formula, there is absolutely no background color where both pure black and pure white fail AA. One (or both) will always pass.

Take #2277d3 (a medium blue). It sits right on a mathematical knife-edge where both black and white actually pass AA (both hit roughly 4.58:1). contrast-color() will hand you whichever has the slight mathematical edge.

But here is the actual gotcha: the WCAG 2.x math has known perceptual blind spots. That same #2277d3 with black text mathematically passes AA, but to human eyes, it can be incredibly difficult to read. contrast-color() gives you mathematical compliance, which is great for automated audits, but that doesn’t always equal perceptual accessibility. (This is exactly why APCA exists and why the spec was designed to let browsers swap algorithms later.)

Furthermore, if you’re aiming for the stricter WCAG AAA standard (7.0:1), a true dead zone does exist. For backgrounds with a luminance between roughly 10% and 30%, neither black nor white will hit 7:1. In those cases, contrast-color() can’t save you — it just hands you the “least bad” failing option.

If you’re animating a background from white to black on hover:

The background fades smoothly over one second. But because the Level 5 output is a discrete value (black or white), the text color can’t be interpolated. It snaps.

And here is the visual gotcha: the snap doesn’t happen halfway through. If you’ve been building themes for a while, you probably have muscle memory from the old Sass days, where we checked if lightness($bg) > 50%. That relied on HSL lightness, where 50% is the geometric midpoint.

But WCAG 2.x relative luminance is a non-linear scale. Under the WCAG formula, the mathematical tipping point — where black and white have identical contrast against the background — actually occurs at approximately 18% relative luminance (specifically ~17.9%).

Because of that, the visual behavior during a white-to-black fade is heavily skewed. The text doesn’t snap in the middle. It stays black for the vast majority of the animation, only snapping to white at the very tail-end of the transition when the background gets extremely dark. It’s a jarring, late hard cut.

You might assume transition-behavior: allow-discrete fixes this. It doesn’t. allow-discrete does not fix the jarring visual experience because it cannot interpolate a binary output; it only shifts the timing of the hard snap to the 50% mark of the animation duration. If you need smooth text color transitions, you’ll have to layer color-mix() or manage the crossfade yourself.

If the background is a perfect middle gray where both black and white produce identical contrast ratios, the spec has a hardcoded tiebreaker: white wins. Not a big deal in practice, but worth knowing if you’re debugging gray palettes and the text isn’t doing what you expect.

The function takes a flat value. You can’t pass it a gradient or a url(). contrast-color(linear-gradient(...)) is a parse error. If your background is a photo or a complex gradient, you still need JavaScript or manually color-pick for overlay text.

Pass a semi-transparent color, and the browser blends it against an assumed opaque canvas (usually white) before running the contrast math. It’s not ignoring your alpha channel — it’s compositing it. But the result might surprise you if you expected the function to “see through” to whatever’s actually behind the element.

If a user enables Windows High Contrast, the forced-colors: active media query kicks in and the browser aggressively overwrites author-defined colors. contrast-color() bows out — forced system colors like CanvasText take over completely. You don’t need to write manual media queries to undo your contrast logic; the browser handles the hierarchy.

Black or white sounds limiting, but once you feed that output into other CSS color functions, you can build an entire component palette off a single custom property.

Pure black text on a vibrant card looks fine. Pure white on a coral card can feel flat. What if the contrast text was a very dark or very light tint of the background color instead?

Kevin Hamer explored related territory in his CSS-Tricks piece “Approximating contrast-color() With Other CSS Features”, where he used OKLCH lightness and round() to approximate the black/white switch without contrast-color() — essentially oklch(from round(1.21 - l) 0 0). That’s a polyfill strategy: get the binary light/dark decision working in browsers that don’t support the native function yet. What we’re doing here is different — we start with contrast-color()’s native output and then enrich it by injecting the background’s own hue:

When contrast-color() returns white, l is 1 (full lightness). When it returns black, l is 0. By pulling the background’s hue back in and adding a touch of chroma, you get text that reads as a deep dark indigo or a pale icy indigo instead of generic black/white. Hamer’s approach gives you the black/white decision without browser support; this one takes the decision the browser already made and gives it personality.

Fair warning: By tweaking the lightness and chroma of the black/white output, you can push a borderline contrast ratio into failing territory. Always run your tinted output through an accessibility linter before shipping.

Also worth noting: This example chains two very modern features — contrast-color() and oklch(from ...). If either one isn’t supported, the entire declaration fails silently. Your @supports block needs to test for both:

Similar idea, simpler API. Mix the sharp black/white output back into the background to soften it:

One custom property driving text, border, and potentially box-shadow or outline. Change --alert-color and the entire component recalculates.

This pattern also works well for ::placeholder text, which is a common pain point in dynamic theming. Placeholder text should be readable but visually softer than the input’s main text — color-mix() with contrast-color() gets you there:

50% mix gives you a muted but legible placeholder that adapts automatically to whatever background the input sits on.

For apps that support system light/dark mode:

When the operating system switches to dark mode, --surface resolves to #121212, and contrast-color() returns white. No media queries, no JavaScript theme detection. The whole chain resolves natively.

The practical payoff: every one of these libraries existed because CSS couldn’t do contrast math. If you’re only using them for readable-text-color selection, you can pull them out of your runtime entirely:

You might still need these for generating complex color scales, but the contrast-for-readability use case is now covered natively.

Beyond bundle size, there’s a performance angle that’s easy to overlook. Those JavaScript libraries don’t just cost you network bytes — they run on the main thread. Every time a theme changes or a component mounts with a dynamic background, your JS has to parse the color, compute luminance, decide black or white, and write the result back to the DOM. That’s main-thread work competing with layout, event handlers, and everything else your app is doing. contrast-color() moves all of that into the browser’s native style computation phase — heavily optimized C++ that runs before paint. For apps with lots of themed components, that’s a real difference in responsiveness.

There’s also a subtle bug that goes away: hydration flash. In React or Vue SSR apps, the server renders HTML without JavaScript. The client then hydrates, running JS to calculate contrast and inject the correct text color. For a brief window between initial paint and hydration, the text is either invisible or the wrong color. Moving contrast into CSS eliminates that entirely — the browser resolves the correct color during the initial paint, before JavaScript loads.

Sass era. You’d write a function that checked lightness($bg) > 50% and returned black or white at compile time. Worked for static themes. Completely useless for user-picked colors, CMS palettes, or dark mode, because the output was baked into the CSS file and could never change at runtime.

The variable toggle hack. When CSS custom properties shipped, people got creative. GitHub used a version of this for their issue label picker — splitting colors into --r, --g, --b channels, calculating Rec.709 luminance inside calc(), multiplying by negative infinity, and clamping to 0 or 1. It worked. It was also unreadable, unmaintainable, and would break silently if you got one parenthesis wrong. (Kevin Hamer’s OKLCH-based approximation is the most elegant version of this lineage — cleaner math, better perceptual alignment — but it’s still a workaround for a function that now ships natively.)

contrast-color() replaces all of these approaches with a single function call. And because the spec lets browsers upgrade the underlying algorithm, your code won’t need to change if and when a successor to WCAG 2.x contrast math lands — whether that’s APCA or something else entirely.

That 70% failure rate was never about developers refusing to care about contrast. It was about the distance between caring and shipping — the library, the build step, the runtime calculation, the hydration flash, the one component someone forgot to wire up. Every gap in that chain was a spot where accessibility quietly dropped out.

contrast-color() doesn’t make developers care more. It makes caring cost nothing.

#9460. Restoration of Brutalist tower in France offers critical lessons in working with concrete heritage

The Perret Tower is a symbol of the 1925 International Exhibition of Hydropower, and of 20th-century architecture Photo: Auriane Poillet; © Ville de Grenoble

An iconic tower built for an international exhibition shaped a French cityscape and tested the possibilities of a new construction material. This is not, however, a reference to the Eiffel Tower but to the Perret Tower, a landmark in Grenoble, the largest city in the French Alps.

Built in 1925 by the concrete pioneer Auguste Perret, the 90m-high beacon was closed in 1960 and stood neglected for 60 years. But this July, a seven-year, €15m restoration returned the building to its original state while rethinking how 20th-century heritage buildings should be renovated.

Standing alone in the middle of Paul Mistral Park, a 15-minute walk from the old town, the tower had become a stranger to its neighbours. “Some thought it had been built for the 1968 winter Olympics,” recalls Cédric Avenier, a Grenoble architect. He has spent decades championing the tower’s rejuvenation to local politicians and the media.

Built for the 1925 International Exhibition of Hydropower and Tourism, the tower offered visitors an unparalleled panorama over the surrounding mountain ranges. For politicians and entrepreneurs, its construction opened a window on a new landscape of opportunities: quick, efficient and cheap building capable of reaching prodigious heights thanks to a new material—reinforced concrete.

“It is the ultimate construction material for the early 20th century: industrial steel and concrete are a match made in heaven,” Avenier says. “They have the same reaction to temperature, the same expansion coefficient. But when this relationship isn’t nurtured, the divorce can be quite brutal.”

The breakup occurs when the natural decay process of concrete—called carbonation—reaches the steel reinforcement, exposing it to humidity and corrosion. The rusting metal expands and bursts the concrete, triggering a vicious, destructive cycle. This affliction was everywhere on the tower’s pillars, jeopardising its structural integrity. The classic heritage restoration process for older stone monuments of singling out, removing and replacing the damaged parts could not be applied here, as concrete is a whole, and should be treated as such.

Before restoration, the Perret Tower served as a unique laboratory for concrete decay. Exposed to the elements, air pollution and temperature fluctuations on all sides and at varying heights, the monument was carefully monitored for a year. “We learned a lot, like how reinforced concrete reacts to temperature drops,” Avenier says. “We also witnessed how quickly concrete decays—in a matter of months.”

Openwork concrete is a distinctive feature of the tower Sylvain Frappat; © Ville de Grenoble

After this observation phase, the project tested various restoration options. The two-year-long, full-scale experiment on two of the tower’s pillars yielded unexpected and unorthodox results.

Out of the four processes tested, the one ultimately chosen—concrete spraying—was the most destructive and had never before been used in a heritage project. The engineering technique is often used in cliff stabilisation and addressed the most important issue for early reinforced structures: the thinness of the concrete coating on the steel, which accelerates the metal corrosion process.

The process required removing 6cm of the original concrete, then placing new steel reinforcements deeper into the pillar. Less exposed to decay and rust, this new structure ensures the tower’s stability for the coming decades. “The technique seemed like an oddity at first glance,” Avenier admits, but adds: “Either we kept the original material, with decaying parts and structural issues, or we had a more intrusive but stable intervention. With concrete buildings, preserving implies removing.”

The Perret Tower renovation challenges some of the dogmas enshrined in the 1964 Venice Charter for the Conservation and Restoration of Monuments and Sites, such as the preservation of original materials and the reversibility of any work undertaken on a heritage site. But the Perret Tower conservation project respects the listed monument’s original design, thoroughly documented in the original architect’s archive. Drawings of the concrete formwork allowed the wood-plank marks on the pillars—a Perret signature—to be reproduced by stamping them onto the sprayed concrete. The new coating is a mix of cement from a local plant and sand found in alpine valleys, as close as can be to the one used by Perret.

While the concrete heritage restoration field is experimenting with chemical and innovative material solutions, Avenier believes that efforts should now be put into skills and proper diagnosis instead. “The renovation used cheap, common materials, and none of those cutting-edge products,” he points out. “The real value lies in the workers’ abilities and the scientific support for such a project.”

A flagship for reinforced concrete construction in 1925, the tower is now a pioneering example of a large-scale concrete restoration. And for Grenoble, it is a rediscovered landmark that awaits around 40,000 visitors a year.

With 8,000 climbs since the July reopening already logged by the end of summer 2026, attendance figures are on track. “A success, with 60% local visitors,” says Alexis Monge, the city official in charge of culture, who also considers the tower an educational tool. “Twentieth-century heritage is not yet what children are taught to find ‘beautiful’. A reopened Tour Perret will be an asset for our schools, to teach the value and preservation of this part of our past.”

#9459. But I Don’t Remember It That Way

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

What estranged parents and children need to know about memory, harm, and the limitations of our personal stories.

There is one sentence that can stop attempts to repair a tumultuous or estranged parent/child relationship in its tracks. For many, this experience may sound achingly familiar:An adult child is naming a painful experience from their youth, often something a parent said or did that hurt them. They are typically hoping to share the truth of their experience and be met with compassion, accountability, and perhaps an apology or steps toward repair.

“That never happened,” their parent says. Or, a slightly softer “I don’t remember that,” fills the space of the conversation.

Memory isn’t a simple recording of past events, even though we often treat it as one.

At this point, the conversation often dies or escalates into an attempt to litigate two memories that simply do not align. It usually doesn’t go well, and everyone walks away more hurt and confused than they were to begin with.

As family estrangement becomes more widely discussed, one critical question often goes unanswered: What do we do when two people’s memories of being in the same family are profoundly at odds?

For parents and grown children caught in the challenging dance of rupture and repair, a difference in memory is more complicated than it looks.

For parents and grown children caught in the challenging dance of rupture and repair, a difference in memory is more complicated than it looks. One of our greatest tools in these moments is understanding how memory works.The first thing we need to understand is that memory isn’t a simple recording of past events, even though we often treat it as one. As a hypnotherapist, I work with memory and long-held beliefs every day to support clients as they overcome fears and phobias, develop more confidence and trust in themselves, and navigate complicated family relationships.

Change is possible precisely because memory is malleable—while we may not be able to change our past, we can change the way we relate to it. This change ripples outward into our lives.

Over time and with the right support, the critical voice of a parent that we’ve carried for decades can begin to quiet, or a deeply held belief that we’re not good enough can give way to something new and more helpful. This flexibility is part of what makes healing possible, and also part of why two people can remember the same past very differently.

As memory researchers Kathleen McDermott and Henry Roediger explain, the process of remembering is reconstructive, rather than reproductive.

You might think of it like the difference between multiple iterations of an artist’s painting. Consider an artist like Monet, who painted his famous water lilies roughly 250 times over 31 years. As an artist continues to paint, their experiences, emotions, knowledge, and beliefs influence the look and feel of every painting—even those images of the same pond of water lilies. The same is true for memory. We selectively encode experiences into our memory, and then we reconstruct them every time we remember.

For one person, an important memory may grow stronger, more vivid, and more steeped in meaning over time. This can be especially true for a painful memory that gets revisited over and over, ultimately becoming part of the architecture of a person’s beliefs about themselves and the world around them.

This doesn’t mean the original memory never happened; it means that it has grown in importance and emotional charge over time. The opposite can be true for memories that aren’t deemed important or meaningful. Less significant experiences may never be strongly encoded in the first place, or may grow harder to recall over time.

The parent/child relationship is one that necessarily holds a significant power imbalance…That can create an imbalance in meaning around even the smallest memories.

This is especially important when we’re talking about differences in memory between parent and child. We remember events in part according to the meaning and emotional significance that they held for us at the time. The parent/child relationship is one that necessarily holds a significant power imbalance: a child depends on their parent for safety, emotional regulation, belonging, and survival, in a way that the parent simply does not. That can create an imbalance in meaning around even the smallest memories.

I’ve seen this with clients on both sides of estrangement. A parent shouting at a child for making a mess, being too sensitive, or doing poorly on a test may not register long-term for the parent while becoming a core part of the child’s narrative. Conversely, parents I have worked with may remember an entirely different version of reality—not the yelling or the critical remarks, but the stress they were under while working multiple jobs or going through a rough divorce.

Both memories reflect something real about each person’s experience, but because of the power imbalance, the impact may have been profoundly unequal. Any parent or adult child trying to repair their relationship needs to understand this. In fact, research also shows that memories of harm are often asymmetrical: people tend to remember being harmed more easily than harming others.

Sometimes “That didn’t happen” is deliberate denial or gaslighting, and sometimes psychiatric or neurological conditions can distort a person’s perception or recollection of events.

Because of this and more, most families at some point will encounter dissonance between memories of important events. There are, of course, important exceptions. Sometimes “That didn’t happen” is deliberate denial or gaslighting, and sometimes psychiatric or neurological conditions can distort a person’s perception or recollection of events. These situations require a different lens than the ordinary differences in memory I’m describing here.

While our memories may never be identical, that probably wasn’t the point in the first place. When an adult child shares a painful memory with a parent, they are rarely asking for a forensic accounting of the past. More often, they are asking their parent to understand something about how they felt or what it was like to be them in that moment. What matters most here isn’t whether both parties can perfectly reconstruct and confirm the facts behind a memory. It’s how that memory is treated.

What matters most here isn’t whether both parties can perfectly reconstruct and confirm the facts behind a memory. It’s how that memory is treated.

Does the parent empathize and get curious, or do they immediately make the case that the child is wrong? Can they pause and acknowledge the potential impact of the memory, even if they don’t remember it clearly? Can they take responsibility where it’s possible to do so? Sometimes, something as simple as “Wow, I don’t remember that clearly, but it sounds really painful. I’m sorry,” can be the springboard into a relationship with more room to grow.

On the flip side, can the grown child leave some room for the possibility that a parent may not remember the same event, not out of malice, but out of the fallibility of memory itself? When we understand this, we can explore with less reactivity.

Ultimately, repair doesn’t require that we come to an exact and agreed-upon version of the past. While we may never remember the same moment in the same way, we can become curious about why it mattered, about our impact on each other, and what we can do now in the present moment to repair.

Juliana Sloane is a Buddhist teacher, hypnotherapist, and coach. She blends ancient wisdom traditions, hypnosis, and evidence-based approaches to help individuals transcend the limitations of talk therapy to create lasting transformation beyond the conscious mind. Based in Santa Fe, NM, she teaches nationally and works one-on-one with clients worldwide.

#9458. How to End the Year with Purpose

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

As the year winds down, we can find ourselves consumed with the busyness of the holiday season, in the thick of responsibility at work and school, and perhaps wondering if we are just spinning our wheels, glancing back to see where the time has gone.

For productivity expert and author Tiago Forte, the Annual Life Review has become an anchor in his yearly rhythm, providing clarity and direction for a life lived with intention. Grab a journal and a pen, a copy of Forte’s latest book, Life in Perspective: The Art and Power of the Annual Life Review, and make deep self-reflection a gift you give to yourself each year.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Life in Perspective.

Tiago Forte: I've been a content creator, coach, teacher, and author for the last 13 years, focused on helping people become more productive with technology. I decided to write this book because I realized over those years that being productive is not helpful if you don't have a clear sense of where you're going and why.

Modern technology is an incredibly powerful force for getting what you want, but you have to know what you truly want in the first place; otherwise it will just fill your time with distraction and noise. My personal answer to this need for deeper intention has been a practice called the Annual Life Review, which I've followed every year for the last 17 years, and this book is my attempt to make it available to others who feel the same need for clarity and balance in our rapidly changing world.

Q: How has practicing an annual life review impacted your own life? In today’s fast-paced world where many of us are seeking answers online, what is the value of looking within for the validation, direction, and inspiration we need?

Tiago Forte: There are endless sources of external information that we're flooded with every day, all year long: podcasts and videos we consume, the advice of gurus and media personalities, and the digital feeds that seek to dominate our attention on every platform.

The annual life review is about turning down the volume on all those external sources and tuning in to internal ones instead – our inner voice, our intuition, our desires, our dreams. No one else can tell us what is right for us, in our unique life circumstances, or what we need to feel fulfilled and joyful. The only source for those kinds of answers lies inside.

The benefit of finding those answers, which I've experienced again and again, is a sense of deep calm, peace, certainty, and self-confidence that I know where my life and career are headed.

Q: What is the method that you disseminate in this book, and how can readers apply it to their own reflective practice?

Tiago Forte: When I first started conducting annual reviews, there was no method or framework to help me structure them. So my process was haphazard and filled with mistakes and wrong turns. Later on, when I learned that many others also practiced year-end reviews of some kind, there was still no definitive book or method to follow.

Annual Review Course (ARC) is the one I developed over the years, first for myself, and later for the students in my course. It takes you on a learning journey from the past, through the present, and finally to the future, where all the insights and realizations you gleaned from the past and present can inform your future plans.

Q: What role might reading and journaling play in this process of annual life review? How have reading and writing helped you to grow, personally?

Tiago Forte: Reading and journaling play a crucial role in the annual review, alongside many of the most proven practices that many people are already familiar with, like meditation, reflection in nature, visualization, and goal-setting.

What the annual life review does is place all those practices into a framework so they build and compound on each other. This leads to an experience that is more than the sum of its parts – a crescendo of insight and meaning that no single one can produce on its own.

Q: How do you hope Life in Perspective changes readers’ lives for the better?

Tiago Forte: I hope it gives them a counterbalance to the fear, uncertainty, chaos, and mental fragmentation that modern life often creates in our lives. A special time and place that they know they can set aside once per year, or anytime they want to return to themselves, and reliably reach a state of balance and clarity. I hope it introduces them to a wider global community of reviewers, from whom they can learn and be inspired. I hope it becomes a cornerstone of their self-reflection and provides a foundation of intention for years to come.

The decision between writing your own will and hiring an attorney is not about cost — it is about complexity. A DIY will is perfectly appropriate for a large percentage of Americans, but certain situations demand professional legal counsel.

If your situation falls into the DIY-appropriate category — which covers roughly 70-80% of American households — you can create a legally valid will for free or under $200 in about 30 minutes.

The online legal services market has matured significantly, and several platforms now produce wills that are functionally equivalent to what a basic estate planning attorney would draft. Here is a detailed comparison of the leading options:

Our recommendation for most FI-focused households: Trust & Will offers the best balance of comprehensiveness and value. The $159 individual plan ($259 for couples) includes your will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney — the three essential documents every adult needs. FreeWill is excellent if you want a basic will at zero cost and do not need power of attorney or trust options.

All of these services work the same way: you answer a series of guided questions about your family, assets, beneficiaries, and wishes. The platform generates a state-specific legal document that you print, sign in front of witnesses, and store. The questionnaire approach actually reduces errors compared to attorney-drafted wills because the software forces you to address every required element.

A legally valid will must contain specific elements. Missing any of them can result in your will being thrown out by a probate court, which means your assets are distributed according to your state's default intestacy laws — not your wishes.

Your will does not control assets with named beneficiaries. Life insurance proceeds, 401(k) and IRA accounts, joint bank accounts, and property held in joint tenancy all pass directly to the named beneficiary or surviving co-owner regardless of what your will says. This is the single most important point that DIY will makers must understand. If your 401(k) beneficiary form names your ex-spouse, your ex-spouse gets the money — even if your will says otherwise. Review ALL beneficiary designations as part of your estate planning process.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The number one estate planning mistake for people building wealth is outdated beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and life insurance policies. Your will does NOT override these. If you changed jobs, got married, divorced, or had children since you last updated your 401(k) and IRA beneficiary forms, update them today. This single action prevents more estate planning disasters than any other — and it costs nothing.

Holographic wills are recognized in about 25 states including California, Texas, Virginia, and North Carolina. They must be entirely in your handwriting, signed, and dated. However, they are far more likely to be challenged in probate because they lack witnesses and often contain vague or incomplete instructions. A typed, witnessed will from an online service is always more reliable than a handwritten one, even in states that accept holographic wills.

No. You do not file or register your will while you are alive. The will is submitted to probate court after your death by your executor. During your lifetime, store the original in a secure, accessible location and tell your executor where to find it. Some states allow you to file the will with the court for safekeeping, but this is optional and not required for validity.

Review your will every 3-5 years and update it after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary or executor, significant change in assets, or moving to a new state. A codicil (amendment) can handle minor changes, but for major revisions, creating an entirely new will is cleaner and reduces the risk of confusion or legal challenge.

Yes. All major online will makers include guardian nomination for minor children. This is one of the most important reasons to have a will — without one, a court will decide who raises your children based on state law, which may not align with your wishes. Name a primary guardian and an alternate, and discuss your decision with the chosen guardians before finalizing the document.

If you die without a will (intestate), your state laws determine who inherits your assets. Typically, everything goes to your spouse and children in proportions set by state statute — which may not match your wishes. Unmarried partners receive nothing. Close friends and favorite charities receive nothing. The court appoints an administrator (who may not be the person you would choose) and the probate process takes longer and costs more. For parents of minor children, the court also decides guardianship.

Writing a will without a lawyer is straightforward, affordable, and legally valid for the majority of American households. Online will makers like Trust & Will ($159) and FreeWill (free) produce state-specific documents in 15-30 minutes that cover everything a basic estate needs. The key to a valid DIY will is proper witnessing, specific beneficiary language, and a residuary clause. Just as importantly, review and update the beneficiary designations on all your retirement accounts and life insurance policies — these override your will and are the most common source of estate planning failures. The only thing worse than a bad will is no will at all. Do it this month.

#9456. Early Medical Pain Can Produce a Lasting Memory

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Several years ago, I worked with a woman who experienced trauma on the first day of her life. She was born with Rh incompatibility, a potentially deadly condition that occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby and her immune system attacks the baby's red blood cells. This woman required a blood transfusion in which all of the blood in her body was drained and was replaced with transfused blood. This medical procedure saved her life, but she is experiencing lasting psychological adverse effects from the trauma associated with this procedure.

As a medical student, I remember watching an infant with his arms and legs strapped down to a board in order for the doctor to perform a circumcision. As the baby cried and screamed, the doctor performing the procedure said that the young boy would not remember this procedure years later. No anesthesia was used. Was the doctor correct? I have wondered about this for more than 40 years, and I can tell you that my research into epigenetic memory has taught me that he was probably wrong.

As a father, I took my 2-year-old daughter to a routine pediatrician's appointment for a vaccination. She cried after the shot, but otherwise seemed OK. The doctor told us she would probably have a sore leg the next day, but Tylenol would take care of it. Well, the next day, our daughter wouldn't walk on her sore leg. She cried and cried, despite our efforts to manage her pain with Tylenol and Ibuprofen. Well, years later, our daughter grew up to be one of the most courageous women I know. She climbed every 14,000-foot mountain in Colorado—all 58 of them! But she has had to deal with a lifelong fear of needles. If she has blood drawn, she has to lie down because she is likely to pass out if she sees the needle. For years, I have wondered: Is her fear of needles related to that early vaccination?

For much of the 20th century, physicians believed that newborns didn’t feel pain. Infants commonly underwent surgery with little or no anesthesia. That belief began to change in 1987, when a review published in The New England Journal of Medicine showed that newborns can experience pain, and they can also experience powerful stress responses due to the pain.

This raises the question: Can pain experienced early in life create a memory that persists for years? Research involving epigenetic memory suggests it is possible.

Epigenetics refers to chemical modifications that alter how genes are expressed without changing the DNA sequence. These modifications help cells “remember” what has previously happened.

In 2004, a study in Nature Neuroscience showed that rat pups receiving little maternal care developed epigenetic modifications to a gene in the hippocampus that left them with exaggerated stress responses as adults. Five years later, another study found similar changes in the brains of suicide victims who had been abused as children. These studies suggested that early trauma can be remembered by modifications to our cells’ DNA.

Strong evidence in humans linking medical procedures to epigenetic change comes from studies involving premature infants. These babies may undergo about 10 painful procedures per day, including heel lances, needle sticks, intubation, and suctioning.

An Italian study found that very preterm infants exposed to more skin-breaking procedures showed increased changes to the serotonin transporter gene between birth and discharge. Serotonin helps regulate mood, anxiety, and pain. A follow-up study linked these changes to greater negative emotionality at 3 months of age.

These changes may persist. Researchers in Canada found that at age 7, children born very preterm had greater epigenetic changes than full-term peers. Neonatal pain predicted that epigenetic changes were associated with more behavior problems later in life. This same group later connected greater neonatal procedural pain to physical changes in the brains of these children at the age of 8.

Healthy, full-term infants are not immune to these trauma-induced changes. Newborn circumcision is one of the most common surgical procedures performed in the United States, and historically it was often done without anesthesia.

In a 1995 study, researchers noticed that circumcised boys cried longer and showed more pain behavior during vaccinations at 4 to 6 months of age than uncircumcised boys. Their prospective 1997 study confirmed it. Circumcised infants reacted more strongly to routine vaccination months later than those who had received a topical anesthetic before circumcision.

In other words, a single painful event in the first days of life appeared to change the infant’s pain system, and pain relief partly prevented it. Whether epigenetic changes underlie this effect has not been directly tested, but the pattern of lasting sensitization from early pain fits closely with the previously described findings.

Toddlers and school-age children remember procedures as well. A review found that a minority of children develop posttraumatic stress symptoms after surgery, and 12 to 31 percent of children undergoing cardiac surgery develop posttraumatic stress disorder. Medical fear in childhood can also shape how people approach health care as adults.

The evidence is preliminary that these changes are due to epigenetic memory. But it is encouraging to note that epigenetic changes appear to be potentially reversible, and maternal sensitivity can reduce these effects in full-term infants.

Necessary procedures should not be avoided because of fear. But the evidence argues that we should be taking infant and child pain seriously. Strategies for reducing the effects of painful and other traumatic procedures include providing anesthesia for circumcision and analgesia for other painful procedures, offering skin-to-skin contact, or breastfeeding during needle sticks, avoiding unnecessary procedures, and preparing older children for what to expect.

The infant may not remember the procedure. But their body may.

#9454. Embracing Discomfort: The Surprising Path to a Meaningful Life

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Discover how engaging in challenging yet meaningful activities can lead to a more fulfilling life. Psychologist Diana Hill shares six strategies to help you lean into discomfort, cultivate resilience, and expand your flexibility.

There are a lot of paradoxes in psychology—the harder you try to fall asleep, the less likely you will; the more you try to avoid thinking negative thoughts, the more likely they will pop into your head; and according to newer research, your greatest meaning in life can come from your greatest pains.

As a clinical psychologist specializing in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), I’ve spent many therapy hours straddling the spaces of pain and meaning. As Steven Hayes, founder of ACT, shared with me on Your Life in Process Podcast, “You hurt where you care.”

Let’s try an experiment to illustrate this coupling. Consider the following activities: Go through the list below, mentally check off those that are both uncomfortable and meaningful.

Which activities did you check? What else would you add? Where else in your life do you do difficult things that are also important to you? If you value caring for your body, you’ll need to face the discomfort of physical activity, and if you value self-respect you’ll need to say no even if it disappoints others.

What is Discomfort Tolerance? The mindful practice of working with difficult feelings rather than avoiding them, recognizing that meaningful growth often requires discomfort.

Core Insight: A meaningful life isn’t free from discomfort but comes from pursuing what matters despite difficulty.

The more you engage in meaningful activities, the more likely you are to experience discomfort. If you love someone or something, you might know this by now. Not only is discomfort associated with purposeful activities like parenting, service work, owning a pet, and social justice, but experiencing pain can be pleasurable in its own right.

For example, hot yoga, deep tissue massage, eating spicy food, and running long distances can be enjoyable because, according to Paul Bloom, author of The Sweet Spot: The Pleasures of Suffering and the Search for Meaning, they create contrast, provide a break from self-rumination, and socially signal strength and competence.

Pain may also play an important role in our dopamine balance. Anne Lembke, the author of Dopamine Nation and chief of the Stanford Addiction Medicine Dual Diagnosis Clinic, shared with me that when we hyperstimulate pleasure centers of the brain with dopamine, we end up experiencing more dysphoria.

Our brain seeks homeostasis by upping our pain to balance out too much pleasure. Taking a “dopamine detox” and residing more on the pain side of the equation paradoxically resets our brain to experience pleasure more fully.

As a therapist, I ask my clients to choose pain in the service of supporting what is most meaningful to them. Exposure therapy is at the foundation of some of the work I do, and much of it is based on the principle of moving toward pain to increase your “zone of flexibility.” With exposure, you flexibly welcome what is uncomfortable when it allows you to live a richer and fuller life.

Most mornings, I get up early to run, lift heavy things, or practice sitting in silence—all in the service of health and well-being. If someone were to force me to do any of these activities, I might feel misery. Having a choice is a powerful psychological tool. Choosing to experience pain instead of resisting it changes your relationship with it. You can even take on the mindset of choice with activities that feel “inflicted on you” by shifting your mindset to “yes brain,” as Dan Siegel calls it. Consider attending a social event: How would your relationship with the event shift if you changed your mindset to choosing to be there versus being “forced” to go? Choose to take a step toward what is uncomfortable, especially when what you care about is in the same direction.

When we are experiencing pain, we often are so engrossed in avoiding it or being overwhelmed by it we lose track of what’s important in the moment. . Imagine you have two dials—a pain dial and a meaning dial. When you turn the meaning dial, it automatically turns the pain dial. They are tethered! Should you turn down the meaning dial? Of course not. Instead, we can practice making space for discomfort while focusing on the meaning dial’s benefits. You may have greater distress tolerance and resilience when focused on meaning and purpose.

Often the anticipation of pain can be worse than the pain itself! Our minds can tell us terrible stories about what is coming next. When choosing to enter an uncomfortable situation, stay in the present moment with the discomfort: Just this minute, just this moment. Present-moment focus helps free you from your mind’s doom and gloom about the pain that is to come. You do not need to tolerate future pain; you just need to accept the discomfort of this moment. Now, that is doable.

One way we try to control pain is to worry and ruminate. Physicializing is an effective practice to help you get out of your head and into the sensations of your body. When you notice a physical or emotional discomfort, try turning toward it in your body. How might you describe the discomfort’s shape, color, movement, or weight? By turning toward and observing your discomfort, you do three things: You give your mind a job other than ruminating and worrying; you develop an observer-self who can recognize you are not your pain even as you experience pain; and you befriend your discomfort. Pain is less scary when you welcome it.

When your threat system is activated, you tend to get a narrowed focus on danger and negative stimuli. Instead of getting caught in tunnel vision, try taking perspective on your experience by zooming out a bit. When else have you done something hard that was meaningful? How did the discomfort change over time? You can also take perspective on the common humanity of discomfort. Building mastery, growing relationships, and learning new skills are uncomfortable for everyone. Remember that discomfort is part of the human experience.

Another reason to choose pain is because it benefits more than just you. Acts of service–choosing to stand so an elder can sit, choosing to drive less so our planet can breathe, or chosing to speak up about injustice–can be uncomfortable. And choosing to practice compassion in relationships can be painful at times. When you choose pain in the service of compassion, you grow a more resilient, courageous mind and heart. No one is immune to suffering and our suffering is interconnected. Turning toward the suffering of others with the energy of compassion, understanding, and care is the greatest gift you can give to another being and to our planet.

Pain and discomfort are part of a well-lived life. Practice opening yourself to your full experience, and you may discover greater freedom.

Diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill
