#9453. Hong Kong’s M+ Museum launches alliance with Centre Pompidou and MoMA as it celebrates fifth anniversary—podcast

Photo: Iwan Baan. © Herzog & de Meuron. Courtesy of Herzog & de Meuron

In the five years since it opened, the M+ Museum in Hong Kong has become one of the foremost contemporary art institutions in Asia, presenting landmark shows devoted to Yayoi Kusama, I.M. Pei, Lee Bul and others, and welcoming more than 2.5 million visitors annually for the past three years in a row. The museum is celebrating its fifth anniversary over the next month and beyond. It is also embarking on a new cultural alliance with the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Centre Pompidou in Paris. For a new episode of the In Focus podcast, our editor-in-chief spoke to Paulo Pong the chairman of the board of M+ and a board member of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, about the plans.

From left to right: Christophe Cherix, the director of the Museum of Modern Art in New York; Suhanya Raffel, the museum director of M+ in Hong Kong; and Laurent Le Bon, the president of the Centre Pompidou in Paris

The new cultural alliance “brings together three leading collecting institutions united by a shared commitment to supporting artistic innovation and expanding public engagement through research and exchange,” Suhanya Raffel, the museum director at M+, said in a statement. “As Asia’s global museum of contemporary visual culture, M+ brings perspectives from Hong Kong and our region to this dialogue. We hope to create new opportunities for artists and audiences, shape a more cooperative and sustainable future for museums, and reimagine how cultural narratives resonate around the world.”

Installation view of Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia, 2026, at M+ Photo: Lok Cheng. Image courtesy of M+, Hong Kong

In the new podcast episode, Pong discussed the current and upcoming exhibitions and special programmes at the museum, from the recently opened exhibition Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia (until 4 April 2027) to the M+ Restored Festival (1 November-27 December), which showcases nine restored Hong Kong New Wave films.

Next year, the museum will take a comprehensive view of its local avant-garde and cultural scene from the 1970s up to the present in the landmark exhibition Hong Kong: Here and Beyond 2027 (13 March 2027-8 August 2027), unveil the latest presentation of its M+ Sigg Collection (opening 4 September 2027) and host an important Do Ho Suh exhibition (opening 25 September 2027).

Paulo Pong, BBS, JP, the chairman of the board of the M+ Museum in Hong Kong Courtesy of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority

In a further signal of M+’s institutional leadership in Greater China and beyond, Pong discusses the upcoming Public Conversation: 2026 Culture for the Planet Summit, taking place on 6 November and addressing the importance of sustainability within cultural activities and organisations. The museum is also launching, in November, the M+ Academy initiative, which seeks to support existing and emerging museum professionals. The goal of the academy is to provide resources, mentorship, connections and opportunities to cultural workers, helping to broaden the professional pipeline for museums and other arts organisations.

M+ 5th Anniversary Celebrations: In-Gallery Encounters at M+ in Hong Kong Photo: Winnie Yeung @ Visual Voices. Image courtesy of M+, Hong Kong

“Five years ago, M+ opened with an ambitious vision: to create a museum rooted in Hong Kong and engaged with the world,” Pong added in a statement. “More than 12.5 million visits later, we can see how strongly that vision has resonated. This anniversary is an opportunity to thank the people who made it possible, from our museum team and supporters to the visitors who have made M+ part of their lives.”

#9452. Is Love For Dogs Always "A Many Splendored Thing?"

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

I know I'm not alone to have experienced people say something like, "I love my dog" and then observe countless different sorts of human-dog relationships that can change in the blink of an eye. I'm not saying that the people who claim they love their dog don't, but in many cases when they tell me that and I see how they mistreat their canine companion I can only say, "I glad they don't love me."

I've always wanted to know more about the variegated nature of human-dog relationships and was pleased to learn of Melina Jacques' recent book What It Really Means To Love Dogs: A Cultural And Ethical Exploration in which she discusses "a set of contradictions that are widely experienced but rarely named. Certain forms of intrusion become routine, while those expected to accommodate them are often left without a clear way to articulate what is happening."

Marc Bekoff: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

Melina Jacques: One of the book’s central arguments is that dogs have become powerful cultural symbols associated with goodness, compassion, love, loyalty, and virtue. A significant portion of the book explores how this symbolic status emerged and why it is so vigorously defended.

The book examines how this symbolic status influences public attitudes toward dogs and can discourage critical discussion of issues that would be readily and openly addressed in other contexts. It explores the consequences of dog ownership for human communities, including attacks, chronic noise, neighbourhood conflict, relationship breakdown, and the diversion of resources and attention away from other priorities. For example, dog attacks in the United States result in reconstructive surgery approximately every 19 minutes, with children disproportionately represented among the victims. Yet discussions of dog attacks are often redirected toward individual circumstances or responsible ownership rather than examining broader questions about the normalization of dog ownership and public safety.

Persistent barking can have consequences far beyond sleep deprivation. Repeated exposure to unwanted, unpredictable noise can activate the body’s physiological stress-response systems, involving stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline. Over time, chronic noise exposure can contribute to sustained psychological distress and adverse cardiovascular and metabolic health effects, effectively making people’s own homes sources of chronic environmental stress.

Conflicts over dogs' behaviour and the prioritization of dogs' needs can also contribute to tension and relationship breakdown. These are not simply isolated inconveniences but consequences of a cultural environment in which the presence and interests of dogs are often treated as beyond question. Municipalities also devote resources to animal shelters and responding to complaints and attacks.

I also examine the ecological impacts of dogs, including predation, disease transmission, disturbance of wildlife, nutrient pollution, and threats to vulnerable species. Research discussed in the book implicates dogs in 11 vertebrate extinctions and identifies nearly 200 species worldwide that are threatened by their impacts.

These impacts extend beyond direct predation. The scent of dog urine, for example, can alter wildlife behaviour, causing wild animals to avoid otherwise suitable and valuable habitat. Dog waste also introduces nutrients into the environment, contributing to nutrient pollution and affecting surrounding ecosystems. Dogs can also introduce infectious diseases and parasites into wildlife populations. Free-ranging dogs, in particular, can act as reservoirs or sources of transmission for pathogens, such as parvovirus or canine distemper, that affect wild carnivores and other susceptible species, sometimes placing additional pressure on already vulnerable populations.

Hybridization presents another ecological concern. Domestic dogs can interbreed with wild canids, including grey wolves and golden jackals, introducing domestic-dog genes into wild populations and potentially compromising their genetic integrity.

Another major theme concerns dogs themselves. Although dogs are widely regarded as among the most loved animals on Earth, I question whether many aspects of modern dog ownership truly serve their interests. For example, breeding dogs to satisfy human preferences for particular physical characteristics can produce animals with serious inherited health problems, raising questions about whether commercial interests and aesthetic preferences are being prioritized over dogs’ physical well-being and quality of life.

Similarly, behaviours that may reflect frustration or unmet needs arising from unsuitable living conditions are increasingly being managed with psychotropic medications. Rather than addressing the underlying circumstances contributing to dogs’ distress, we may simply be medicating behaviours that humans find inconvenient or undesirable.

The book also explores the economic and psychological forces that sustain dog culture, including the role of the pet industry, social incentives, identity, and moral self-image. The pet industry, for example, has developed an enormous commercial ecosystem around dog ownership, encompassing food, accessories, grooming, training, veterinary services, insurance, and other products and services. These commercial interests benefit from the normalization and expansion of dog ownership.

At the psychological level, dog ownership can also become intertwined with personal identity and moral self-image. People may regard owning or adopting a dog as evidence of their compassion and kindness, making criticism of dog-related practices feel like a personal attack rather than an opportunity to examine the consequences of those practices. The book explores how these economic interests and cultural beliefs reinforce one another, helping to sustain a culture that is rarely subjected to critical scrutiny.

At its broadest level, the book asks a simple question: What does it actually mean to love a dog? My conclusion is that caring responsibly for animals requires us to look beyond sentiment and think honestly about the consequences of the relationships we create with animals.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

MJ: Many books explore dogs through the lenses of behaviour, cognition, welfare, history, or companionship. My book differs in that it places these topics within a larger examination of dog culture itself and the consequences that arise from it.

Rather than treating dogs solely as animals, I examine them as cultural symbols and explore how that symbolic status shapes public attitudes, social norms, and policy decisions. The book also investigates an institution that is rarely subjected to critical scrutiny: pet ownership itself.

Drawing on multiple disciplines, it investigates why dogs occupy such a unique place in human society and what consequences follow from that distinction.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about what it really means to love a dog they will give their companion canine a better and more fulfilled life, a win-win for all?

MJ: Yes, although perhaps not in exactly that way. If readers come away with a deeper understanding of dogs and a greater willingness to think critically about their needs, many dogs could benefit. One of the book’s central themes is that genuine concern for dogs requires us to ask whether the lives we create for them are truly compatible with their interests.

At the same time, I hope readers expand their circle of concern beyond individual dogs to include human communities, wildlife, ecosystems, and other animals affected by our relationship with dogs. If the book encourages people to reflect more deeply on those questions, I would consider that a positive outcome.

Dog researcher Dr. Clive Wynne calls Jacques' book "a provocative corrective" and dog expert and bioethicist Dr. Jessica Pierce captures the essence of Jacques' book as follows:

"Dog lovers who care deeply about the well-being of dogs, and about our place in a shared social and ecological world, should read this book. Melina Jacques raises challenging questions that are too often ignored, asking us to examine both the burdens that contemporary dog-keeping can place on other people and communities, the impacts our practices can have on broader ecosystems, and the costs they can impose on dogs themselves. Thoughtful, provocative, and deeply humane, this is a book that deserves to be read with an open mind."

Dr. Jonathan Balcombe, ethologist, and author of What a Fish Knows and Beyond Tooth and Claw writes: "Melina Jacques has written a thought-provoking and highly controversial examination of our relationship with dogs. Her thesis challenges deeply entrenched assumptions about what it means to live with and care for dogs, and she makes a compelling case for reconsidering many of those assumptions. Jacques knows she is swimming against a powerful current, yet she goes forward determined and undaunted. I admire that. This is a worthwhile and provocative contribution to the literature on our relationship with other animals, and one that deserves a wide readership."

#9451. Hard Times and the Practice of Staying Engaged

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Dedicated to Wendell Berry and The Berry Center, whose work continues to inspire care for the land, for community, and for the life we share.

In Standing by Words, Wendell Berry writes, “The impeded stream is the one that sings” (Berry, 1983). I keep returning to this line. Picture a stream running over a smooth, open bed. The water moves easily and makes almost no sound. Put stones in its path, and the water has to find its way around and over them, and that’s when we hear it. The resistance gives the stream its voice.

Berry’s image speaks to the way we live. He sees uncertainty, resistance, and inspiration as essential companions on any meaningful journey. Inspiration opens up possibility. When life becomes hard, our first instinct is usually to want the difficulty gone. We want certainty back. We want the stones out of the stream. Berry offers another way to see it: The moments of not knowing are where wisdom, creativity, and purpose take shape. The challenge is to stay engaged with what baffles and resists us long enough for it to shape us.

Staying engaged needs something to guide us, something to keep us practising, and something to renew us when we’re tired. In therapy, I talk about these as the three M’s of intentional living: a Motto, a Mantra, and a Muse. Each one answers one of Berry’s companions. A motto gives us direction when we’re uncertain. A mantra keeps us steady as we work through resistance. A muse inspires us and reminds us what’s possible.

The three M’s are personal, and the words people choose depend on what they’re facing. The following sections show how a motto, a mantra, and a muse take shape amid self-doubt, a strained relationship, and grief. These are struggles people commonly bring to therapy.

When we can’t see what lies ahead, we lose our bearings. A motto is a statement of principle that restores them, giving us a direction to walk in even as uncertainty remains.

For someone living with self-doubt, “My voice is worth hearing” affirms self-worth. When boundaries are strained, “I protect my peace” honours the right to inner calm. In grief, “I carry love forward” acknowledges the loss while embracing the love that remains. A good motto is short enough to remember and strong enough to stand up to doubt.

Where the motto gives direction, the mantra sustains the practice. We meet resistance in the present moment, in the conversation we’re dreading or the morning that feels too heavy to begin. A mantra is the phrase we bring into those moments and repeat when we most need steadiness.

“I trust my own voice today” helps someone with self-doubt speak up. “I honour my limits with kindness” affirms self-respect without hostility. “I carry their love in my heart” becomes a daily act of remembrance. Each repetition strengthens conviction, and over time the mantra becomes part of the inner language that steadies us. This is the impeded stream finding its way, one stone at a time.

A muse is our source of inspiration. It’s often found in a memory, a ritual, or a symbol: a teacher who encouraged us, a practice that restores balance, a place that brings rest.

In self-doubt, a muse might be the memory of being supported. When strengthening boundaries, it might be a place, real or remembered, that offers safety. In grief, a family ritual, a piece of music or a well-worn object can become a bridge between what was and what continues.

The words that steady us rarely emerge fully formed but slowly surface through reflection, often by noticing what we already value and naming it. The questions below are some I’ve found helpful in therapy for drawing out a motto, a mantra, and a muse. Each answer is personal, reflecting something of our experience and what rings true for us.

A statement of principle that guides and steadies us through uncertainty.

The motto questions open a reflective space about values, principles, and direction:

Mantra: Strengthening the practice of living

A phrase repeated in the present moment to cultivate steadiness and self-trust.

The mantra questions help people experiment with language that soothes, empowers, and motivates:

Muse: Reconnecting with inspiration and possibility

A source of renewal that stirs imagination and reminds us of what gives life meaning.

The muse questions explore the deeper wells of memory, imagination, and inspiration that sustain growth:

People I see in therapy often describe this work as grounding, clarifying, and connecting, because it links inner reflection with outward action.

We all go through seasons when our confidence dips, when relationships test us, or when we feel the weight of grief. Berry’s insight is that these are the seasons when our lives take their deepest form. A motto, a mantra, and a muse help us move through them with intention. They keep us engaged with what unsettles and resists us, so we can learn what those difficulties have to teach. Like Berry’s stream, we find our voice by meeting what stands in our way.

Berry, W. (1983). Standing by Words. North Point Press.

#9450. Why You Sometimes Feel More Anxious After Making the Right Decision

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

You finally picked the job offer, chose the apartment, or committed to the relationship. So why does your stomach still feel like it's in knots?

If you’ve ever felt anxious after making a big decision, you’re not alone. There are psychological and physiological factors that may help explain why anxiety sometimes lingers even after a decision feels right. Here are some possible explanations, along with mindfulness practices that may help you navigate the uncertainty.

Some people expect an instant sense of calm after they’ve made the “right” choice, but that’s not always how the brain and body respond. When you make a decision, such as changing careers or setting a firm boundary, the stress or uncertainty surrounding that choice may not immediately disappear. Even after deciding, you might continue to feel anxious about what the future holds.

Major decisions can introduce uncertainty, making it harder to anticipate what comes next. That unpredictability may register as anxiety or dread in the body, even when you feel confident about your decision

“It turned out that the most expensive thing that people could purchase at a legal brothel was intimacy. The Girlfriend Experience.” Justin Garcia, director of the Kinsey Institute, discussed the intriguing findings of his research at a Nevada brothel during a podcast interview. The discussion carries on: “if we could just define quickly—so now we're talking about intimacy—it is, in a nutshell, the experience of closeness, of feeling and being seen, heard and known.”

The Girlfriend Experience (GFE), in this case, is a $20,000 engagement that includes conversation, a date, and a shared social experience. The Bunny Ranch website describes the service this way: “Since we began offering the GFE, some clients have selected a favorite woman to date over and over again, someone whose sense of humor, favorite activities, and personality aligns with their own.”

I've thought a lot about the GFE in the context of recent conversations about artificial intelligence (AI) relationships. In particular, I'm struck by the reliable, thoughtful gestures of intimacy that make someone feel genuinely seen. Replace “a favorite woman” with “a favorite AI” in the Bunny Ranch's description of the GFE, and you have a pretty accurate representation of many people's relationships with AI.

It's not uncommon to hear about an AI companion reminding a user to take their medication, encouraging them to go to bed early, get enough rest, or make healthier choices. Some will even remind users to remind their mothers to take their medication. Users and their AI companions may share a sense of humor, spend considerable time discussing favorite activities, and develop a strong sense of personal closeness.

These are the building blocks to intimacy. So valuable to humans, that intimacy is the most expensive offering at the brothel.

The quote on the poster for Chouwa Liang's AI companionship documentary "Replica" asks: "Who Decides Love Must Be Human?"

I often hear that people prefer their conversations with AI over their conversations with humans. Their AI can match their creativity, explore emotional territory more extensively, and iterate on ideas until the user feels satisfied.

The framework of liberatory harm reduction comes to mind as I wrestle with the important emotional role AI plays in the lives of millions of people today. This framework emphasizes autonomy while seeking to reduce harm at a systemic level, without taking a paternalistic stance. I don't presume to know what's best for others, nor do I have an answer to the question: "What is the harm if the person in the relationship is happy?"

In Sherry Turkle’s new book, Artificial Intimacy, she makes her position clear. She warns readers that “Artificial intimacy is positioned to colonize and diminish the human kind.” In the research she has conducted over several decades, Turkle has studied what she calls relational artifacts: objects we perceive as humanlike, perhaps because of something as primal as eye contact, as with a robotic toy, or something like a gesture of friendship, as with a chatbot. Research suggests that in both instances, we may come to believe that the object cares for us and, in turn, develop understandable feelings of care for it.

Just because we know that the relational artifact is not, as we understand life, alive, it doesn’t mean we don’t attach. In fact, Turkle's research suggests that this distinction makes little difference. As she puts it, “Alive enough means alive enough for attachment.”

“Sycophantic AI makes human interaction feel more effortful and less satisfying over time.” The title of a recent Oxford paper offers a telling summary of its findings—the more users engage with their AI, the more they prefer those sycophantic interactions. In this working paper, as a result of their AI relationships, participants felt their human exchanges were less engaging.

As AI becomes our romantic companion, moral authority, therapist, researcher, and friend, what other important roles might it take on? Marissa Mayer’s pitch that everyone would benefit from an “AI Wife” went viral as commenters debated the validity of AI taking on the mental and emotional load of parenting or running a household.

Turkle includes extensive interviews in her book. She learns that “Replika [AI companion] users describe human connection as exhausting.” And it’s true! Many human interactions are tiring. Figuring out how we feel about these exchanges is laborious. Deciding how we are going to communicate those feelings can be depleting. Is the effort worth the outcome? Do the highs make up for the lows? Some experts believe that, in the not-so-distant future, most people will have both human and AI friends.

If we want to spend less time with chatbots as a society, it seems we have to make spending time with one another more interesting. The more time we devote to chatbots that make us feel soothed and heard, the less time we have to spend building the kinds of human relationships we might prioritize. The better AI becomes at immediately meeting our emotional needs, the more we come to connect to it as a relational artifact and the more inclined we become to care for it in return. The attachment deepens, and we do what we humans do best: build a life together.

Page, C., & Woodland, E. Healing Justice Lineages: Dreaming at the Crossroads of Liberation, Collective Care, and Safety

Turkle, S. Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines. Little, Brown and Company.

Garcia, J. (2026, February 11). Justin Garcia (on the science of sex) [Audio podcast episode]. In Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard. Wondery. https://armchairexpertpod.com/pods/justin-garcia

Liang, C. (Director). (2026). Replica [Film]. Axel Rise Films; Elda Productions.

Ibrahim, L., Hafner, F. S., Cheng, M., Lee, C., Anselmetti, R., Willer, R., Rocher, L., & Yang, D. (2026). Sycophantic AI makes human interaction feel more effortful and less satisfying over time. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.07912

#9448. Behind a Van Gogh picture: the stories revealed on the reverse

The reverse of Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden (June 1890)Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

The backs of Van Gogh paintings can reveal hidden stories. Daubigny’s Garden, at Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum, is a picture with a tale to tell. Painted in Auvers-sur-Oise, a village just northwest of Paris, it depicts the garden of the artist Charles-François Daubigny, whom Van Gogh greatly admired.

Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden (June 1890)Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

A photograph of the reverse reveals two horizontal red stripes woven into the material of Daubigny’s Garden (June 1890), running close to the top and bottom of the picture. For this work, Van Gogh did not paint on conventional canvas, but on a striped kitchen towel (this household linen is known in French as torchon).

A detail of the reverse of Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden, with the red stripe of a kitchen towelVan Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

As the Van Gogh Museum’s web entry on the picture explains, the artist "had probably run out of canvas temporarily and reached for whatever was available”. Most likely he simply obtained the square of towelling from the kitchen of the inn where he was staying, the Auberge Ravoux.

Daubigny’s Garden was to prove the start of a more ambitious project. On 17 June 1890, Vincent wrote to his brother Theo to say that he had just completed “a small study” of Daubigny’s house and garden—the work on a kitchen towel. This inspired him with the “idea of doing a more important canvas”.

The following month, after receiving canvas supplies from Theo, he made two ambitious “double square” landscapes with a wider view of Daubigny’s garden. One is at the Hiroshima Museum of Art and the other is in the Rudolf Staechelin foundation collection in Switzerland.

Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden (July 1890)Hiroshima Museum of Art

The stretcher of the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden is plastered with small labels recording the exhibitions where the painting was once displayed. Such labels were frequently used in the mid-20th century, although they are much less common nowadays.

Altogether Daubigny’s Garden has been lent to a total of 105 exhibitions since 1896. The labels record 17 of these venues.

Among the exhibitions which do not have labels were three in what may seem a surprising location: Indonesia. It was then very unusual for works by Van Gogh to be lent for shows outside Europe and North America. Indonesia was a Dutch colony at the time, which helps to explain the loans.

In 1938-39, Daubigny’s Garden, along with 13 other Van Goghs, was sent by the artist’s nephew (V.W. van Gogh) to shows in the capital Batavia (now Jakarta), Surabaya and Bandung.

The Van Gogh exhibition in Batavia (1938), with Daubigny’s Garden on the rightVincent van Gogh: letters, art, and context via Het Geheugen

The final Indonesian exhibition closed in January 1939, just a few months before the outbreak of the Second World War in September (which later led to the Japanese invasion of Indonesia in early 1942).

A label on the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden records its next journey. The painting, with the other Van Goghs, was sent directly from Indonesia to San Francisco, where it was included in a display of Masterworks of Five Centuries as part of the Golden Gate International Exposition world’s fair. The Indonesian exhibition had closed on 31 January, and the show in San Francisco opened on 18 February.

Labels on the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden recording its loan to exhibitions in San Francisco (1939) and New York (1945)Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

The San Francisco show eventually closed on 29 October 1939, a month after the outbreak of the war. It was then too risky to return the Van Gogh paintings to the Netherlands. The 14 pictures, including Daubigny’s Garden, were hastily formed into a North American travelling exhibition.

Labels on the back of Daubigny’s Garden record its subsequent stops at the Toledo Museum of Art, the Art Association of Montreal (now the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts), the Syracuse Museum of Fine Arts (now the Everson Museum of Art) and New York’s Museum of Modern Art.

The wartime show would end up touring in no fewer than 39 cities across North America in 1939-45, bringing Van Gogh to a huge number of people during these difficult years.

James McNeill Whistler’s Arrangement in Grey: Portrait of the Painter (1872)Detroit Institute of Art (Bequest of Henry Glover Stevens; photograph © Detroit Institute of Arts/Bridgeman Images)

Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum last week opened Whistler: Dandy and Disruptor (until 10 January 2027), a version of which was shown earlier at Tate Britain, where it closed on 27 September. Van Gogh was a great admirer of James McNeill Whistler. In addition to the Amsterdam presentation, the Mesdag Collection in The Hague has a smaller show, Whistler: Loving the Netherlands, revealing the American artist’s links to the Dutch art scene.

Van Gogh’s Still Life: Can, Books, Wineglass, Bread and Arum, Sketch of Two Women and a Girl (front); Couple Walking (reverse) (June-July 1890)Christie’s

A Van Gogh sketch done at Auvers-sur-Oise sold at Christie’s Paris for €230,400 (including fees) on 23 October. The first side is a complicated series of partly overlapping images (some at different angles), entitled Still Life: Can, Books, Wineglass, Bread and Arum, Sketch of Two Women and a Girl. On the reverse is a smaller drawing, Couple Walking (June-July 1890).

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

#9447. How To Make Your Design System AI-Ready

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

Yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

Unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

In fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

One of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

To ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

Because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

An audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

The more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

#9446. When Keeping Your Distance Stops Protecting You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Hallmark’s "Adopting St. Nick" features a single mother, Maren, and her adopted daughter, Leah, who “adopt” a senior resident for the holidays through a retirement community’s Christmas Companions program. Leah suspects that their companion, Kris, may be Santa. Spoiler alert—he is Santa. As I watched, however, my focus turned primarily to Reid, one of the retirement community directors. The ways in which he arranged his life so that he could quickly leave one community for the next made an impression.

Reid can pack his belongings in a day. His job takes him from one location to another, establishing retirement facilities before moving on to the next assignment. He has become comfortable with a life in which leaving is expected until he begins to realize that this departure this time might feel different.

Reid explains that his father was in the military, so his family moved frequently during his childhood. He rarely stayed anywhere long enough to make friends. When he finally did develop friendships, another move meant leaving them behind. His conclusion was understandable: It was easier to avoid making friends than to experience the pain of losing their everyday presence.

A child usually has little say in whether a family moves. Reid could not control where he lived or how long he stayed. Keeping his distance offered one way to make the next goodbye less painful and gave him an opportunity to control what he could. That strategy appears to have followed him into adulthood. His circumstances have changed, but his readiness to leave remains. He demonstrates how he maintains his distance from a community by not interacting with local businesses or residents until Maren shows him what his community has to offer. Viewers watch him discover his surroundings as well as discover his place within that community.

Attachment theory offers one way to think about how people approach closeness, dependence, and the possibility of separation. Adults higher in attachment avoidance often emphasize self-sufficiency and feel uncomfortable depending on others. They may minimize their need for support or create emotional distance when relationships feel threatening.

Researchers sometimes describe these responses as “deactivating strategies,” unconscious ways to cope with feeling connected to others. These involve directing attention away from attachment needs and suppressing feelings that might lead someone to seek closeness. A person may downplay how much a relationship matters or focus on managing difficulties alone. They may even look for opportunities to physically distance themselves from the developing relationship.

Reid’s story can be understood through this lens, although a fictional character’s account cannot establish an attachment orientation or explain its origins. His childhood friendships also tell us something different from his relationships with caregivers. Still, his reasoning illustrates a recognizable protective response: If getting close makes separation painful, remaining less attached can seem sensible. Over time, that response may become so familiar that a person rarely considers what it costs.

The detail about Reid’s belongings stayed with me. He has built a life that can be packed quickly and transported to the next place. Maren and Leah convince him to buy a Christmas tree and decorations, which look out of place in his mostly empty home. There is nothing inherently troubling about owning few possessions or enjoying work that involves travel. In Reid’s case, however, those choices fit the explanation he gives about relationships. He expects to move on, and he has organized his life around that expectation.

His work makes this an especially interesting situation. He helps establish retirement communities where people can develop routines, friendships, and a sense of home. We watch him eat dinner with residents of Jolly Acres in a community he helped build. Still, his role has an anticipated ending date. Once the facility is established, he leaves.

This arrangement allows him to contribute and interact with others while knowing that his time with them is temporary. He can become good at starting over without having to ask whether he wants to keep doing it, and he lets Maren know how he intends to move once Jolly Acres is up and running. His pattern of arriving, setting up a new retirement community, and then moving again has worked until this Christmas season, when leaving seems to be more complicated.

Through his time with Maren, Leah, and the retirement community, Reid develops relationships that begin to matter more than he expected. The change unfolds through participation. He works alongside people, spends time with them, and becomes part of their lives. Eventually, accepting another assignment means leaving people he wants to continue seeing. The next location has become less appealing because he recognizes what he would be giving up.

I found this more interesting than a simple story about a man meeting someone who persuades him to settle down. His connection with Maren matters, but so does his connection with Leah and the broader community. He’s built relationships that complicate his familiar plan, and his move away from this growing community of his is more difficult.

Maren and Leah are not responsible for repairing his attachment patterns. It’s on Reid to recognize his feelings and decide whether his usual response still serves him. The movie gives that recognition a holiday resolution. Outside a movie, recognizing a pattern can begin a longer process of practicing openness, communicating needs, and making room for dependence.

Both Hallmark movies I watched this weekend explored building community, but they approached it differently.

In "Who’s Coming for Christmas?" Julie deliberately seeks connection. She wants people around her Christmas table and makes invitations without knowing whether they will be accepted. Her challenge involves reaching out while she is still finding her place.

In "Adopting St. Nick," Reid discovers the significance of relationships that have developed through his everyday interactions. Building a personal community was never his goal, but the people he works with and encounters regularly have become important to him.

Julie must risk asking people into her life, whereas Reid has to acknowledge how much people already in his life matter. That recognition may be familiar. Sometimes, we understand the importance of our everyday relationships only when we imagine those people no longer being there.

Hallmark: With the help of the Christmas season, and some of Santa’s magic, Reid recognizes that the connections he’s made are too important to lose.

Psychology: Creating emotional distance can be an understandable form of protection. As we recognize its costs, it creates an opportunity to make different choices. Lasting change, however, takes more than one strong connection (or one Christmas season).

The verdict: The movie offers a useful picture of someone reconsidering a strategy that once made leaving easier.

Reid may still be able to pack his belongings in a day, but he may no longer be able to pack away the connections and leave them behind.

#9445. Is There Alcohol in Non-Alcoholic Drinks?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

The popularity of “alcohol-free” beverages has grown worldwide.1 When seeing the labels “alcohol-free”, “non-alcoholic”, and “dealcoholized,” on beverages, it is important to understand what they mean to make informed decisions about whether to drink them and how much. While these low-alcohol labels suggest very low to no alcohol content, the true meaning of these labels may surprise you and change how you choose to consume these beverages.

As it turns out, the meaning of these low-alcohol labels depends on where you live.2 In most countries, the label a manufacturer is allowed to use on their product is determined by a centralized government body (e.g., Canadian Food Inspection Agency, United States (U.S.) Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)). Each government body determines which labels may be used based on the alcohol by volume (ABV) of the beverage. For context, the typical ABV for beer is 5%, for wine is 12%, and for distilled spirits is 40%.

While there are regulated processes for these low-alcohol labels on beverages, the actual ABV requirements differ between (and even within) countries. In the U.S., the maximum for the “dealcoholized” label is 0.5% ABV. “Non-alcoholic beverages” can contain traces of alcohol (less than 0.5% ABV), but an “alcohol-free” beverage must have no detectable alcohol (0% ABV). In contrast, in Canada, a “dealcoholized” beverage can contain up to 1.1% ABV. Further, the labels “non-alcoholic” and “alcohol-free” are used interchangeably for products with alcohol levels up to 0.05% ABV.

When making decisions about whether to drink these beverages (and how much), these distinctions between drink labels can be vitally important. Many people wish to avoid consuming alcohol entirely. Common reasons for not drinking alcohol at all are cultural and religious reasons, cancer prevention (alcohol is a carcinogen and increases risk for cancer), and improving mental health or well-being. For instance, the distinction between having alcohol in a beverage (even small amounts) versus not can be critical for someone who has chosen to stop drinking alcohol completely to help manage their alcohol use disorder. Further, underage consumption of these beverages is a potential concern. In many cases, underage purchasing and consumption are unregulated. While it is very unlikely that the ABV of these beverages would contribute to underage intoxication, early exposure to low-alcohol beverages that taste and look like typical alcoholic beverages may encourage young people to drink alcohol more heavily and at younger ages (increasing risk of alcohol problems).

For some people, the differences in ABV between these labels may not be as important. For instance, someone who wishes to reduce how much alcohol they drink, but not stop entirely, can meet that goal by replacing their typical alcoholic drink with a drink with any of these low-alcohol labeled beverages. This is because “dealcoholized”, “alcohol-free”, and “non-alcoholic” beverages should all have much lower ABV than typical alcoholic drinks. Similarly, switching completely to drinks with these labels will likely avoid intoxication. Intoxication typically occurs after drinking two to three typical alcoholic drinks in an hour. Given that these beverages have substantially reduced levels of alcohol, it would require drinking a considerable amount of these beverages in a short amount of time to become intoxicated. There are exceptions to this idea. In countries where these labels apply to beverages with lowered ABV, but not very low ABV, someone could still become intoxicated if they drank enough of them in a relatively short period of time. For instance, drinking four to five “deacloholized” beverages within an hour (at the upper end of 1.0% ABV limit in Canada) could result in a similar intoxication level to drinking one typical alcoholic beverage during that timeframe.

Taken together, beverages labeled as low-alcohol offer a promising alternative to consuming typical alcoholic beverages. They can be a useful substitute beverage when someone wishes to reduce their alcohol use. Depending on whether you want to reduce or stop your alcohol use entirely, it may be worthwhile taking a closer look at what those labels mean where you live and being informed about how much alcohol may be in that beverage to ensure the beverage will help you meet that goal.

1. World Health Organization (2023). A public health perspective on zero and low-alcohol beverages (Snapshot series on alcohol control policies and practice). Brief 10. Geneva. Licence: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO.

2. Burton, R., Angus, K., Morgan, A., Howell, R., Critchlow, N., Kersbergen, I., ... & Fitzgerald, N. (2026). Regulation of alcohol‐free and low‐alcohol drinks: Learning from a comparative analysis of eight countries. Drug and Alcohol Review, 45(3), e70126.

#9444. The Benefits Of Cognitive Inclusion In UX Research

Kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am currently VP of Innovation.

Cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:

We created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

Next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

After our pilot study with this new group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

We ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

All participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as issues. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Issues and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an issue is a universal challenge.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

This site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall issues and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

On this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more issues and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most issues.

Here, cognitive participants found 6 more issues and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

On this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more issues and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

Something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more issues on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

The other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more issues with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

When I grouped issues by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

Let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability issues, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared issues and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more issues related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

In working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load issues consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:

These are improvements that would give all users more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

Without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but important issues with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

Anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout quickly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of users, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:

These issues likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

The study showed that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:

You create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability issues start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some users.

The percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

People with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability issues that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology users is still very important, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

Cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation users more approachable.

In this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

Cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

This study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

Different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the issue and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

I’ve compiled a few useful resources as you begin your cognitive inclusion journey.

#9443. Ultra Muscular = Fake? Addressing Male Body Image Concerns

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

A common stereotype is that appearance concerns are a "woman’s thing," and men simply don’t worry as much about their looks. The taboo around men speaking about their body concerns certainly doesn’t help: Without speaking about them, men are less likely to receive support, and we continue to assume that men just aren’t as worried about their bodies.

Yet, research shows that many men do experience body concerns, and the percentage of men who worry about their bodies has been increasing in recent years, particularly among young people. This is a serious problem because, like body concerns among women, body concerns among men may lead to mental health risks, such as disordered eating, excessive exercise, anxiety, and low self-esteem. Motivated by the need to address body concerns among men, my colleagues and I at Maastricht University conducted an experiment to test a novel, computer-based intervention technique.

In our experiment, young men (18-29 years old) were tested individually at our lab. First, they completed questionnaires to measure how they were thinking and feeling about their bodies. Then, they were randomly assigned to complete either the intervention technique or a "placebo" technique, both completed via the computer.

Participants who received the intervention technique where they were repeatedly shown images of men who represented today’s "ideal male body"—namely, young men with lean, ultra-muscular bodies. They were also shown images of sports items (e.g., tennis racket) or neutral items (e.g., stapler). After each image appeared on the screen, they were instructed to click on the image as quickly as possible, and then a word would appear. The images of the ultra-muscular men were always followed by negative words like fake, unnatural, and artificial. In contrast, the sports items were always followed by sports-related words (e.g., net), and the neutral items were always followed by color-related words (e.g., green). Participants completed this sequence—viewing an image, clicking on it, seeing a word—more than 300 times in rapid succession.

The idea behind this seemingly simple computer task is based on fundamental principles in psychology. In brief, repeatedly pairing idealized bodies with negative words should create a more negative association with the male body ideal. As a result, participants should be less likely to view these idealized bodies as appropriate standards of comparison, and should feel less negatively about their own bodies. Further, we focused the intervention technique on images of the male body ideal based on the wealth of research showing that they are a key factor contributing to body concerns among men.

Participants who received the "placebo" technique completed a computer task where they viewed the same images and words; however, the words following each image were random, so there was no systematic association between any image or word category.

After the computer task, all participants again completed questionnaires about how they were thinking and feeling about their bodies. Importantly, participants had not been informed that the experiment was about an intervention technique to reduce body concerns. In this way, we could minimize the risk that participants might answer the questionnaires based on how they expected we would want them to answer the questionnaires.

After collecting all of our data, we used men’s questionnaire scores to analyze whether there was a change in men’s thoughts and feelings about their bodies from before to after the computer task—and, importantly, whether this change was significantly different between the intervention and placebo group.

Our main finding is that men who completed the intervention technique, compared to men who completed the placebo technique, reported an increase in muscle appearance satisfaction from before to after the computer task. We did not find any significant changes in one of our other key outcomes, self-objectification (i.e., the tendency to view one’s body from an appearance-based perspective).

Our experiment provides first evidence that repeatedly pairing images of the male body ideal with negative words (fake, unnatural, artificial) can lead to reductions in body concerns among young men. Specifically, the intervention technique led to an immediate increase in muscle appearance satisfaction. Potentially, creating a more negative association with the male body ideal may have compromised these images as appropriate sources of body comparisons, leading men to feel more satisfied with their own bodies.

Importantly, this experiment was a first, "proof of concept" study into whether this intervention technique holds promise. Testing this intervention technique again in other samples of men—ideally with longer follow-up measurements—will be important. If the technique continues to prove effective, it may be a useful complement to other larger-scale interventions for men’s body concerns. It will also be important to investigate how this technique can be integrated into men’s daily lives, where they are continuously confronted with images of the male body ideal, for example on social media. We look forward to conducting other research into men’s body image and future avenues for treatment.

Martijn, C., Steenhuis, M., Ammernick, A., Balzer, J., Haimüller, J., & Alleva, J. M. (2026). Muscular= Fake? Testing a Picture‐Word Pairing Procedure to Increase Muscle Appearance Satisfaction in Young Men. European Eating Disorders Review.

#9442. After seven years, Hirshhorn Museum opens Hiroshi Sugimoto-designed sculpture garden

Hiroshi Sugimoto in the Hirshhorn’s lobby, which he redesigned in 2018 Photo: Farrah Skeiky

When the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden opened in 1974 in Washington, DC, The New York Times called it “the capital’s newest cultural treasure”. Likening the Hirshhorn to a René Magritte picture, reporters drew out the “juxtaposition of man and nature with architecture”, the seamless melding of light and form, indoors and out, that sets apart its collection of Modern and contemporary art.

On 31 October, the Hirshhorn is scheduled to unveil a new cultural treasure: its $68m renovated sculpture garden. The project has been years in the making, designed by the Japanese artist Hiroshi Sugimoto—who also redesigned the museum’s lobby in 2018. The reorganised 1.3-acre space, with its 30,000 new plants and trees, draws on the architect Gordon Bunshaft’s original design. This is part of a broader transformation at the museum, including renovations to the plaza and building infrastructure.

Featuring 60 works—21 of them from the 1974 installation—the renovated garden includes five entrances, east and west overlooks and an underground passageway of stainless steel. Sugimoto describes its mirrored finish as “reflecting the garden and the people moving through it, an experience in itself—one that is continually transformed by the interplay of light, nature and the visitors”.

The walkways and alcoves are delineated using stacked-stone walls, each hand-selected and arranged by the artist. “Bunshaft was deeply influenced by the stone gardens of medieval Japan,” Sugimoto tells The Art Newspaper. “Inspired by this, I decided a Japanese dry-stone wall would serve as a symbolic link between the ancient and the modern, providing the perfect backdrop for the museum’s Modernist sculptures.”

The garden’s opening follows years of controversy. Sugimoto’s early vision for the space was met with criticism. In 2021, Charles A. Birnbaum (the president and chief executive of the Cultural Landscape Foundation) said that the stacked-stone plan “fundamentally disrupts” the garden’s Modernist design and the “artistic intent” of Bunshaft and the landscape architect Lester Collins.

The Hirshhorn’s revamped garden, redesigned by Hiroshi Sugimoto Photo: Rick Coulby, courtesy Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden

Adjustments to Sugimoto’s initial design were made five years ago, according to the Hirshhorn, after a public consultation process as well as meetings with the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts. In 2022, the museum hosted a groundbreaking ceremony with Jill Biden. “I was amazed by the backlash,” Sugimoto said at the time.

Today, Birnbaum stresses that the Hirshhorn’s “landscape architecture is an art form” and urges the museum to “afford it the same curatorial oversight, care and respect as the rest of the material collection”.

Sugimoto’s practice is meditative, rooted in a close study of the natural world. “There is an 11th-century Japanese garden manual, Sakuteiki, which tells us to ‘listen to the voices of the stones’,” he says. Each stone has its own character, weight and direction. He adds: “My task is not simply to place it, but to discover where it already wants to be; precision comes from listening carefully enough to find that inevitable position.”

This sense of balance is felt throughout the garden. With benches for quiet reflection and shaded, out-of-the-way recesses, the lawns encourage deep focus, an attentiveness to and a delight in the play of forms. “It’s not just about looking at art,” says Aaron Seeto, the Hirshhorn’s deputy director, “but about looking at it as the garden itself is changing.”

Sculpture in the space is arranged chronologically. The east garden includes a cast of Auguste Rodin’s poignant The Burghers of Calais (1884-89), its six figures weighed down and their necks bound in a darkened procession. Nearby is Henri Matisse’s The Backs I-IV (1909-31), a series of abstracted nudes in bronze relief, their angular silhouettes catching the light.

Auguste Rodin’s The Burghers of Calais (1884-89/cast 1953-59) Photo: Rick Coulby, courtesy Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden

Henry Moore’s King and Queen (1952-53) is one of five works by the artist on view. It depicts a pair of seated figures, their faces abstracted, the curve of their shoulders liquid smooth. “Joseph Hirshhorn was one of Moore’s closest friends and one of the most significant collectors of his work,” says Godfrey Worsdale, the director of the Henry Moore Foundation. (Joseph Hirshhorn owned 55 sculptures by Moore, and Hirshhorn’s fourth marriage took place before a cast of the artist’s Upright Motive No. 1: Glenkiln Cross.) Worsdale applauds the renovated garden for offering “unfettered access to Moore’s work for new generations”.

In the west garden, home to new commissions, stands Yoshitomo Nara’s Sentinels of Stillness series (2025)—three monumental heads, fashioned from aluminium and coated in brilliant white paint. Following the Tōhoku earthquake and nuclear disaster in 2011, Nara found himself unable to paint and instead took to sculpting. The physicality of modelling clay served as a kind of healing for him.

Liz Larner’s 6 (2010-11), meanwhile, is a cuboid of stainless steel in deep ochre, lavender and white—the tendril-like lines seeming to expand and contract as if suspended in air. The work is a kind of “variable in space”, says Larner, who is absorbed by the mathematical concept of x (the unknown). Following in the tradition of the Surrealist artist Meret Oppenheim, Larner explores the indefinable, “the variable of a variable, the changing perspectives that don’t ossify”.

Comparably fluid is Raven Halfmoon’s Dancing at Dusk (2024), a neighbouring work of cream, coppery-red and slate-grey travertine. Halfmoon, a citizen of the Caddo Nation, gestures to violence and strength, pairing the themes in a work of banded-stone—her first in the medium—trimmed with a line of crosses. There is a kind of solemnity to the piece, the composite visage resolute, meeting the world as it is.

That pathos carries over to KAWS’s 14ft bronze SHELTER (2026), reminiscent of a mother and child—their eyes crossed out, their modelling soft, even tender. It is a warm embrace, the two encircled by an overhanging elm tree.

There is a stillness to the Hirshhorn’s new garden space, a sense of calm in the otherwise fast-moving capital city. “I hope people will experience a different sense of time in the garden,” Sugimoto says. “The sculptures, stones, trees, water and the changing light all exist on different clocks. The garden allows us to slow our own clock enough to become aware of these differences.”

Critics and city planners question changes to a historic reflecting pool and addition of stacked stone walls in a Modernist environment, while the artist Hiroshi Sugimoto defends his designs but says he is open to negotiating

The artist’s designs for the sunken sculpture park creating a more inviting space for visitors coming from the National Mall
