#9427. Why Does Everyone Else's Weight Loss Feel So Personal?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

A friend tells you she's lost 20 pounds. A coworker shows up looking noticeably smaller. Your sister mentions that she's started taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss. You recognize that what they do with their bodies is their decision, but before long, you're thinking about your own appearance. You start wondering whether you've gained weight, studying yourself in the mirror, or questioning what you ate that day. Nothing about your body has changed since yesterday, so why are you suddenly feeling dissatisfied with it?

Weight loss is so widely celebrated that congratulating someone for becoming thinner has become a normal and socially acceptable response. Yet weight loss can happen for many reasons, including illness, depression, stress, inadequate nourishment, or an eating disorder. Even when someone has intentionally lost weight and feels good about it, praising the change reinforces the idea that a smaller body is a better body.

We rarely consider what these compliments might mean to someone who later regains the weight. After hearing how wonderful they looked when they were thinner, they may worry that others now find them less attractive or assume they've let themselves go. Nobody has to make a negative comment about their weight gain for them to feel ashamed. The earlier praise has already communicated which version of their body was considered more desirable.

These messages also reinforce the stigma people with larger bodies face, whose appearance is often used to make assumptions about their health, behaviors, and self-discipline. We have become so accustomed to associating thinness with health and attractiveness, and have been told that everyone can and should control their weight and shape. These beliefs end up pathologizing the natural diversity of human bodies.

I think there's more to these reactions than jealousy, particularly for people who have struggled with eating disorders or chronic dieting. Seeing someone else lose weight can bring back memories of when changing your body felt like the solution to so many things you were unhappy about.

Think about all the things you may have missed out on because you felt bad about your body. Perhaps you avoided swimming with friends because you didn't want to be seen in a bathing suit, made excuses not to go to parties because you felt uncomfortable with how you looked, or refused to buy clothes you liked until you went down two sizes. You kept promising yourself that you'd do these things once you were thinner. Looking back, there's sadness in recognizing how many experiences you missed while waiting to feel comfortable in your body.

For someone recovering from an eating disorder, watching another person receive praise for losing weight can bring back memories of the approval they once received. You may remember feeling accomplished when the number on the scale went down, even though maintaining that weight required behaviors that were harming you. It can be upsetting to miss those feelings, especially when you remember how miserable you were at the time.

Eating disorder recovery involves questioning beliefs about food, weight, and self-worth that are deeply embedded in our culture. Sometimes those old thoughts resurface, particularly when the people around you celebrate the very thing you've worked so hard to stop pursuing.

Talk about weight loss has always been difficult to avoid, but the widespread use of GLP-1 medications has brought even more of these conversations into everyday life. People share stories about medications, compare how much weight they've lost, and discuss changes in their appetites. Even a simple dinner can turn into a conversation about portion sizes or how little someone is eating.

In my work as a therapist specializing in eating disorders and body image distress, I hear how frustrating this has become for people who have spent years trying to improve their relationship with food. After working to become less preoccupied with eating and weight, they're surrounded by people discussing medications and the pursuit of smaller bodies. Some describe feeling pulled back into a way of thinking they've worked hard to leave behind.

GLP-1 medications have also changed how people think about losing weight. With weight loss increasingly presented as something that can be achieved through medication, those who have stopped pursuing it may begin questioning their decision. There's a growing sense that if changing your body is possible, you should at least consider it. For someone who has worked to accept their body, that pressure can be difficult to resist.

If hearing about someone else's weight loss makes you want to start dieting again, think about what your previous attempts to lose weight were actually like. Maybe you lost weight and felt good about yourself for a while, only to regain the weight, sometimes more than you initially lost. Each time, you blamed yourself for not having enough willpower or discipline and promised you'd do better with the next diet.

Weight regain is common, in part because our bodies respond to weight loss by increasing hunger and conserving energy. Yet when a diet fails to produce lasting results, people tend to blame themselves rather than question the diet. After years of losing and regaining weight, that repeated sense of failure can seriously affect how someone feels about themselves.

It's worth remembering what those years of dieting actually involved. Perhaps you constantly thought about food, felt guilty after eating, or judged yourself based on what the scale said that morning. If you've decided to stop dieting or are recovering from an eating disorder, you likely had good reasons for wanting something different for yourself. Another person's weight loss doesn't change those experiences.

It's understandable to feel uncomfortable when a friend talks about losing weight, especially if you find yourself comparing your appearance to hers. You might even feel envious of the attention she's receiving and then guilty for having those thoughts. Given how much importance our culture places on thinness, these reactions aren't surprising.

Sometimes the way to cope with those feelings and protect your eating disorder recovery is to first pay attention to what happens afterward. Are you checking your body more frequently, reconsidering foods you've been comfortable eating, or thinking about restarting a diet? Recognizing these changes early can help you avoid slipping back into behaviors you've worked to move away from.

It's also reasonable to limit conversations about dieting and weight loss. You can change the subject or tell someone, "I'm trying to spend less time thinking and talking about weight, so I'd rather hear about what else is going on in your life." You don't owe anyone a detailed explanation of your relationship with food or your body.

We can't prevent other people from pursuing weight loss or control how much attention their changing bodies receive. But we can question why someone else's weight loss has become a reason to criticize our own appearance. You don't have to return to dieting, change how you eat, or become smaller simply because someone else has. Their body is theirs, and yours doesn't need to change in response.

#9426. Prediction Markets and Betting on Elections

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Federal law prohibits online gambling platforms such as DraftKings or FanDuel from wagers on election outcomes. On the prediction markets of Kalshi and Polymarket, a person can buy an event contract on an election. This election cycle, nearly $1.9 billion has been traded on these markets.

Both online gambling platforms and prediction markets involve future events. What’s the difference between wagers and event contracts? That may be a distinction in search of a difference. Regardless, the effects of these platforms and markets on individuals, our elections, and democracy matter enormously.

With online betting, a person may place a wager on the outcome of a sports event, a card game, or just about anything else but an election. If a person has a winning bet, the online platform, a.k.a. the house, must pay out. The house has an interest in a particular outcome. To gamble legally online, a person must be at least 21 years old.

In a prediction market, participants buy event contracts about the outcome of future events, which might include sports, military operations, election outcomes, and when a celebrity couple will get married. Prediction markets set prices by probabilities. An event contract selling for $.25 that the local football team will win the day’s game implies there is a 25 percent likelihood of the team winning. Purchasing an event contract is a financial transaction and not a wager. Participants in a prediction market trade directly with the other participants. The market is neutral on the outcome. Kalshi charges a fee for each transaction, but they do not pay out like the house does with gambling. This is the crux of the argument that prediction markets are not a form of online betting. To buy event contracts, a person must be at least 18 years old.

Tomato, tomahto. I believe that prediction markets are online betting by another name. This form of online gambling poses significant risks to individuals and to our democracy. I have four concerns that weave together.

Nearly 75 percent of Kalshi’s event contracts involve sports. It is young men who are fueling the online betting and purchase of event contracts. The younger a person is when he starts betting, the greater the likelihood of developing a problem with gambling and experiencing gambling-related harm. This may begin with people visiting the platforms more often and spending increasing amounts of time there. Dynamic pricing in the prediction market makes that more likely. When new information is available, public sentiment shifts, or there are changes in risk tolerance, the price of the event contract shifts. These pricing changes keep bettors tethered to the platform and making trades with each other.

The price of an event contract is the result of artificial intelligence (AI) crunching massive amounts of data. Most bettors just look at the results of the crunching, follow those results, and trade their contracts repeatedly. Following along because AI has indicated probabilities is a new version of the bandwagon fallacy. Old-school bandwagon fallacy involves the assertion that a claim is true because the majority of people believe it is true, which prompts more people to hop on the bandwagon. AI now functions as the supermajority for most people, which makes individuals less willing and even able to seek their own evidence and argument.

For those young people who grew up playing video games, online gambling sites will be familiar as entertainment or excitement. Prediction markets allow people to bet on the outcomes of elections as if they were games. Free and fair elections are the backbone of a democracy. Now they are viewed as akin to a sporting event. The stakes are enormously high with elections; their consequences extend for years. Voting affords the opportunity for people to make their voices heard and their preferences known. Young people arguably have the greatest stake in elections because they will have to live with the consequences for longer periods of time. Choosing candidates and buying event contracts based on probabilities of their winning as opposed to their characters or their platforms is not genuine voter engagement.

Betting on elections becomes a matter of an individual’s personal gain from an election outcome. It telescopes a person’s interest in an election to the probability of that person winning a bet. Winning the bet becomes more important than the consequences of the election. I am not naïve to assume that personal interest hasn’t governed people’s voting patterns, but these bets radically change the calculus. A person’s vote will follow the bet. This makes it less likely that people would vote for something beyond their self-interest, such as the well-being of others or the common good.

Prediction markets can harm individuals, the common good, and even democracy itself.

#9425. The Joy of Feeling Small

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Awe doesn't always make us feel bigger or better about ourselves. Sometimes it reminds us of our "small self." We see that we’re part of something bigger—and that can be a relief.

Tap, tap, tap. I’m typing away in a café in North London. Outside, the sky is grey. Around me, people are ordering drinks, looking at their phones and talking through problems with colleagues. There must be about twenty of us in here, each with something on our minds.

I have my own concerns. There’s a pile of admin waiting for me, and I’m not especially keen to get on with it.

I stop typing and look around. Each person has a life as complicated as mine. Someone might be worrying about money. Someone else might be looking forward to seeing a friend. A person across the room could have received wonderful news this morning, while somebody else might be quietly dealing with something awful. We sit alongside one another, sharing the same small space, with no real idea what’s happening in each other’s lives.

#9424. Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

Mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

We know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a

with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

That gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

For years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

But audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple new features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

The WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

Start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And

#9423. Beyond Bars and Into Being

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Midway through the 2024 film "Sing Sing," a group of men rehearses a play in a classroom at a maximum-security prison in New York (Kwedar, 2024). Some of the actors learned their craft while they were incarcerated. They are alumni of Rehabilitation Through the Arts (RTA), the theater program the film portrays, and on screen they play versions of themselves.

RTA makes a striking claim about what happens after its participants go home: only around 5% return to prison (ABC7 New York, 2022). Nationally, 27% of people released from prison are reincarcerated within three years, down from 35% for those released in 2008 (Council of State Governments [CSG] Justice Center, 2024). The national figure is moving in the right direction. RTA’s figure suggests the arts may be reaching people in ways standard rehabilitation misses.

One possibility is that creative engagement addresses barriers conventional re-entry programs tend to overlook: trauma, a disrupted sense of self, and strained emotional capacity. The idea is promising, and the research behind it is still young.

The past two decades have brought new investment in re-entry, including the Second Chance Act of 2008, which funded education, mental health care, and substance use treatment for people leaving prison (CSG Justice Center, 2024). Attending to these needs is valuable; however, far less attention goes to what years inside do to a person’s mind and body. “The legal system, and incarceration more specifically, produces a legacy of intergenerational trauma and health harms,” says Dr. Rebecca Fix, an Assistant Professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “Instead of addressing the traumatic circumstances that led many to incarceration, prisons exacerbate those harms.”

In a study of about 4,000 incarcerated men, 44.7% reported physical trauma in childhood (Wolff & Shi, 2012). Current rates of post-traumatic stress disorder are roughly five times more common among men in prison than in the general population, and about eight times more common among women (Baranyi et al., 2018). Experiences in prison typically perpetuate this trauma and distress. Victimization, solitary confinement, and coercion experienced in prison are each associated with PTSD (Piper & Berle, 2019). Among people released after long sentences, researchers have identified a lasting cluster of symptoms that includes chronic distrust, difficulty making decisions, and trouble sustaining relationships (Liem & Kunst, 2013). Poet Reginald Dwayne Betts was incarcerated at 16 and spent 14 months in solitary confinement. His collection Felon traces how that time follows a person long after release (Betts, 2019). These are the very capacities people need to rebuild their lives at home, work, and in their families, and most re-entry services do little to restore them.

Coming home after prison means building a new story about who one is, one in which a person sees themselves as capable, creative, and worthy of a future (Maruna, 2001). Creative work offers a place to start writing that story (Fleetwood, 2020). For example, Jimmy Santiago Baca (2001) entered prison unable to read and taught himself to read and write there, emerging as a poet. Shaka Senghor (2016), who spent seven of his 19 years in prison in solitary confinement, credits literature and self-examination with helping him confront his past.

Making art engages the body and the senses along with language. In one small study of adults outside prison, 45 minutes of art-making lowered levels of the stress hormone cortisol in about three-quarters of participants (Kaimal et al., 2016). In another study, dance movement therapy lowered depression scores by 72% in 12 weeks (Jeong et al., 2005).

Theater and writing give people a place to try on a new identity. On stage, someone the system calls an inmate becomes an actor, a writer, a member of an ensemble, and an audience watches that change happen. Narrative identity research links redemptive life stories to well-being (McAdams & McLean, 2013), and performance may be one way to rehearse such a story out loud (Maruna, 2001). Ashley Lucas (2020), former director of the Prison Creative Arts Project, draws on years of directing theater in prisons to describe how performance builds community and hope in settings designed to strip both away. In Baltimore, Center Stage launched a year-long theater program in 2024 with young people held at the city’s Juvenile Justice Center (Baltimore Center Stage, n.d.). Stella Adler Studio of Acting has been partnering with the Rikers Island Correctional Facility since 2014. Every week across the year, a cadre of trained artists – including teachers, writers, voice and speech experts, movement coaches and directors – visit multiple facilities to reach hundreds of inmates annually. Ensemble work asks for turn-taking, negotiation, and impulse control, too. In an evaluation of California prison arts programs, participants reported gains in emotional control, time management, and self-confidence, and disciplinary reports fell (Brewster, 2014).

An evaluation of the University of Denver Prison Arts Initiative concluded that arts programs can “invoke liberatory experiences for participants” (Littman & Sliva, 2021, as cited in Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, n.d.), and other studies report fewer depressive symptoms and a greater sense of self-respect and purpose among participants (Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, n.d.).

While peer-reviewed research conducted in carceral systems is thin, though growing, a meta-analysis of arts therapies in forensic settings, including 11 randomized or controlled trials, found improvements in psychiatric symptoms and in social and psychological functioning (Abbing et al., 2023). In a randomized trial with 200 men in a Chinese prison, group music therapy reduced anxiety and depression and raised self-esteem (Chen et al., 2016).

The punitive model assumes that people choose crime and that harsher consequences will deter them. Research offers little support for that assumption: compared with non-custodial sentences, imprisonment has a null or slightly criminogenic effect on reoffending (Nagin et al., 2009). Scholars and organizers including Angela Y. Davis (2003), Ruth Wilson Gilmore (2022), and Mariame Kaba (2021) call for moving resources away from prisons and toward the people and institutions that help communities thrive.

The arts are one of those investments. “Alternatives to incarceration, including restorative and transformative approaches, ask what people and communities need to heal,” Fix explains. “For many, creative expression is part of that answer, as an alternative to the traumatic carceral environment, though arts programming within prisons can also offer meaningful support where alternatives don't yet exist.” They give people a structured, safe outlet for processing difficult experiences, room to rehearse a new identity, and a way to contribute something others value. The arts also help people who have been incarcerated speak for themselves. Ear Hustle, a podcast about life inside created at San Quentin State Prison by Earlonne Woods, who was then incarcerated there, and artist Nigel Poor, reached a national audience and was a 2020 Pulitzer Prize finalist (The Pulitzer Prizes, 2020).

The arts can be a powerful tool to support the social and emotional health of incarcerated individuals. For the men who learned to act at Sing Sing and then played themselves on screen, creative work was part of how they rebuilt their lives. Far more people leaving prison deserve the same chance.

Maya Lakshman, MPH, is a doctoral candidate at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, where she uses neuroimaging, geospatial, and qualitative methods to understand the impacts of structural and interpersonal violence on development and mental health across the lifespan. She is a writer, educator, and researcher with an interest in translating evidence into equitable, justice-centered public health policy.

Federal student loans offer multiple repayment plans, and choosing the right one can save you tens of thousands of dollars — or cost you the same amount if you choose poorly. The standard 10-year repayment plan is the default and the cheapest option in terms of total interest paid. Every other plan either extends your timeline (increasing total interest) or adjusts payments based on income (providing relief now at a higher long-term cost).

The graduated plan starts low and increases every two years, which sounds appealing for early-career borrowers but costs $3,800 more in interest than the standard plan. The extended plan cuts your monthly payment nearly in half but more than doubles your total interest. Income-driven repayment (IDR) plans offer the lowest payments but can extend repayment to 20-25 years, and the forgiven balance may be taxable income (though this tax treatment is waived through 2025 under current law).

For FI-minded borrowers, the standard 10-year plan or an accelerated payoff is almost always the best choice. Lower monthly payments feel good in the short term but cost you years of investment growth on the other side of payoff.

The most powerful student loan payoff strategy requires no negotiation, no refinancing, and no paperwork — just sending extra money each month. Even small additional payments create dramatic results because they reduce principal directly, which means less interest accrues in every subsequent month.

Here is what extra payments do to a $37,000 loan at 6% interest on the standard 10-year plan.

The math is striking: $100 per month in extra payments saves $4,700 in interest and frees you from student loan debt 3.5 years sooner. That is 3.5 years of $411 monthly payments — roughly $17,300 — that you can redirect to index fund investing instead of sending to your loan servicer.

When making extra payments, explicitly instruct your servicer to apply them to principal, not to advance your due date. Many servicers default to "paid ahead" status, which counts extra payments as future monthly payments rather than principal reduction. Call or submit written instructions that all extra payments must be applied to the principal balance immediately.

The FI angle here is powerful: every month you cut from your student loan repayment is a month your money starts compounding for you instead of against you. A 25-year-old who pays off $37,000 in student loans in 5 years instead of 10 and then invests $411 per month for those freed-up 5 years accumulates roughly $30,000 in additional wealth by age 35.

Beyond extra payments, three strategies can significantly accelerate or reduce your student loan burden: refinancing for a lower interest rate, qualifying for Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), and leveraging employer student loan repayment benefits.

Refinancing replaces your existing loans with a new private loan at a lower interest rate. If you have strong credit (720+), stable income, and a low debt-to-income ratio, you may qualify for rates 1-3 percentage points below your current federal rate. On a $37,000 balance, dropping from 6% to 4% saves about $4,200 in total interest on a 10-year term.

PSLF forgives the remaining balance on Direct Loans after 120 qualifying payments (10 years) while working full-time for a qualifying employer — government agencies, 501(c)(3) nonprofits, and certain other public service organizations. The forgiven amount is not taxable, making PSLF the most valuable student loan benefit available.

To maximize PSLF, enroll in an income-driven repayment plan to minimize your monthly payments during the 10-year qualifying period. Lower payments mean a larger remaining balance at forgiveness — and since the forgiveness is tax-free, every dollar of reduced payment is a dollar you can invest during those 10 years.

A growing number of employers offer student loan repayment assistance as a benefit — typically $100-$300 per month or $2,000-$5,000 per year toward your balance. Under current tax law, employers can contribute up to $5,250 per year tax-free toward an employee's student loans. Ask your HR department if this benefit exists — it is one of the most underused benefits in corporate America and directly accelerates your path to debt freedom.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

When you send extra money to your student loan servicer, they may apply it as an advance on future payments rather than reducing your principal balance. This means you are technically "paid ahead" by a month or more, but your principal — and the interest accruing on it — remains the same. Contact your servicer (by phone and in writing) and explicitly request that all extra payments be applied to the principal balance immediately. This ensures every extra dollar reduces what you owe and saves you maximum interest.

Student loan payoff is calculated using an amortization formula that accounts for your principal balance, interest rate, and monthly payment amount. Each payment covers accrued interest first, with the remainder reducing principal. Extra payments go entirely to principal, which reduces the interest charged in every subsequent month and accelerates your payoff date.

For most borrowers, yes — especially those with rates above 5-6%. Paying off a $37,000 loan just 3 years early saves $4,700+ in interest and frees up $400+ per month for investing. The exception: borrowers pursuing PSLF should make minimum payments to maximize forgiveness, and those with very low rates (3-4%) may benefit more from investing the extra money.

Refinance if you have strong credit (720+), stable income, and no plans to use income-driven repayment or PSLF. Refinancing to a lower rate saves money, but you permanently lose access to federal protections. Never refinance if you work in public service or may need income-driven payment flexibility.

SAVE (Saving on a Valuable Education) is the newest income-driven repayment plan for federal student loans. It caps payments at 5% of discretionary income for undergraduate loans (10% for graduate), provides an interest subsidy that prevents your balance from growing if payments do not cover interest, and forgives any remaining balance after 20-25 years.

Yes, you can deduct up to $2,500 per year in student loan interest paid, even if you do not itemize deductions. The deduction phases out at higher incomes (MAGI of $80,000-$95,000 for single filers). This deduction effectively reduces your loan's interest rate by your marginal tax rate — a 6% loan costs roughly 4.5% after the deduction if you are in the 22% bracket.

Federal student loans are discharged (forgiven) upon the borrower's death or total and permanent disability, with no tax consequences. Private student loans vary — some have death discharge provisions, others do not and may pursue the estate or a cosigner. If you have private loans with a cosigner, consider term life insurance to protect them.

Your student loan payoff date is not set in stone. Extra payments of just $100 per month can cut years off your repayment timeline and save thousands in interest. Use the right repayment plan for your situation — standard 10-year for aggressive payoff, income-driven if pursuing PSLF, and refinancing if you qualify for a significantly lower rate. Every month you cut from your student loan timeline is a month your money starts building wealth instead of paying interest. Debt freedom is the first milestone on the path to financial independence.

#9421. Visual war and the underwater secrets of the Inca

El Huarco’s cliff structures, made by the Inca in the 15th century, were designed to be seen from the sea Rocío Villar Astigueta/Ministerio de Cultura de Perú

Near the desert cliffs of Cerro Azul, 170km south of Lima, visitors are likely to stumble on El Huarco. This is a place where architecture was not merely the result of conquest but served as an aggressive form of visual propaganda, designed to overwrite the history of a vanquished society. Recently, maritime and coastal archaeological research has revealed that an imposing imperial structure, erected by the Inca in the 15th century, was not intended to be seen from land but instead to scare off enemies approaching by sea.

To secure their dominion, the Inca undertook a radical aesthetic transformation of the cliffs, creating a landscape specifically designed to both impress and intimidate. “Recent studies along the bluffs have identified 17 architectural elements,” the archaeologist Rocío Villar Astigueta tells The Art Newspaper, “including walls and orderly lines of stone that provide evidence of the intense modification of the cliff face overlooking the sea.”

She adds that this architecture was deliberately planned to be viewed from the ocean: “Its visibility from the sea acted as a political marker for sailors, communicating the presence and power of the Inca Empire on the central coast,” linking this architecture to a system of ports or paths that formed part of the network of the Qhapaq Ñan (the Inca road system).

El Huarco Archaeological Site Rocío Villar Astigueta/Ministerio de Cultura de Perú

Prior to the expansion of the Inca Empire in the 15th century, the lower part of the Cañete Valley belonged to the Huarco Confederation. The Huarco were master fishers, hydrologists and architects of the landscape. Their architectural language was defined by tapial—massive walls of rammed earth that reflected the dusty shades of the cliffs—and small sun-dried adobe bricks. For centuries, this organic architecture served a proud society that tenaciously defended their autonomy.

In his Crónica del Perú (1553), the Spanish conquistador Pedro Cieza de León describes the war between the Inca and the Huarco as one of the most brutal chapters in the pre-Hispanic history of the Andes. The Inca forces faced stubborn resistance for four years, and their victory ultimately came not through a direct military advance but trickery.

As the story goes, the Inca emperor’s wife used the area’s spiritual traditions to devise a deadly trap. She sent a mission to propose a great ritual ceremony of joint fishing to honour the goddess of the sea, promising the Huarco that the Inca would recognise their sovereignty over the valley in exchange for their participation. The Huarco agreed, abandoning their clifftop fortresses to board the ceremonial rafts. Once the hidden Inca army had left the Huarco defenceless at sea, it entered the valley, took control and captured the population. The Inca hanged the Huarco leaders and most of the local inhabitants.

To create the imposing cliff structure after their successful conquest, the Inca introduced elite stonework techniques to an environment built entirely of earth. Villar stresses that the architectural styles found on the cliffs include imperial masonry with finely rounded and assembled stones, comparable to what is found in the palaces of Cuzco—the historic capital of the Inca Empire. For anyone sailing along the coast, the sight of these enormous stone structures, perfectly fitted together and gleaming on the desert cliffs, held an unmistakable message.

A ceramic sculpture recently found in the waters off El Huarco Rocío Villar Astigueta/Ministerio de Cultura de Perú

Recent archaeological research in the waters just off El Huarco’s cliffs followed reports from local fishers of strange objects and shapes spotted beneath the waves. Peru’s cultural ministry organised groups of divers to see if they could find anything. They discovered submerged stone walls, once part of the coastal settlement (now underwater because of changes in sea level, erosion and earthquakes) as well as Inca artefacts tied to early navigation and fishing. Many of the surfaced artefacts are now held at the nearby Municipal Museum of Cerro Azul.

“The museum’s entire collection consists of objects that residents have voluntarily contributed,” says the archaeologist Astrid Suárez. “The fishermen’s associations also support fieldwork aboard their boats. Children play a crucial role, insisting to their parents that they hand over objects discovered by their grandparents or aunts and uncles and passed down from generation to generation, after learning that this is cultural heritage and we are all responsible for protecting it. The children also act as museum guides in exchange for tips.”

As Peru’s cultural ministry uses some of these new findings as proof of the importance of the site—an effort to eventually declare it Cultural Heritage of the Nation—the cliffs of Cerro Azul continue to bridge the gap between myth and reality. The site remains an enduring monument to the way empires, water and stone can rewrite human history.

The incident at Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas, has drawn attention to the lax security at the 600-year-old Unesco World Heritage Site

A Chinkana, or labyrinth, with three branches has been found beneath the ancient city of Cusco

Radiocarbon dating of human bones and teeth in Peruvian ruins indicate that the Inca first lived at the citadel around 1420, not after 1440

#9420. How to Transform Your Fears Mindfully

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

The only way through your fears is to get comfortable being uncomfortable.

Fear is a part of everyday life. It’s always lurking around, threatening us, horrifying us, on bad days crippling us, and on good days simply annoying us.

There are the mega-fears, both real and imaginary: that someone is following you when you walk alone at night, or that the headache you’ve had for two days actually indicates that something is horribly wrong. More common are little nagging fears that keep you awake at night, eat away at you, and prevent you from experiencing the day around you.

How do we work through all of these sources of anxiety, these situations and stories that force us to bump up against our frailty and finitude?

A simple starting point is to challenge yourself to do things that are unfamiliar and uncomfortable. For me, this approach helps me wake up, calm down, and extend myself.

In the past decade I’ve noticed that physically challenging tasks are the ones that cause the most visceral fear reactions for me: noticing my limitations, and questioning how I can go beyond what I think I can do.

In the past ten years I’ve noticed that physically challenging tasks are the ones that cause the most visceral fear reactions for me: noticing my limitations, and questioning how I can go beyond what I think I can do.

I often refer to my daughter as my personal trainer, because she convinces me to go for hikes and other outdoor adventures that force me outside of my comfort zone. When I go for a hike with her, it’s usually twice as long as my normal limit, and it often takes me over terrain that is more varied and challenging than I prefer. I’m not like an antelope jumping from rock to rock. I’m more like a turtle with a waddle, trying to climb a hill.

I’ve learned to breathe through most of these adventures, when to take a break, and when to push on. I’ve also found that a moment of uncertainty or fear brings instant focus on the present. When I face the first physical challenge on the trail, I’ve noticed consistently that the initial feeling of trepidation slowly dissolves into a feeling of bravery and accomplishment.

So, I recommend the uncomfortable as a way to learn to work with fear. It can be a physical challenge, as described above, or leaning into a relationship or an uncomfortable interpersonal space. As the Stranger in The Big Lebowski says, “Sometimes you eat the bear and sometimes, well, he eats you. “ You don’t always win, in other words, but you learn as much from the mistakes as from the triumphs. And fear will always give you more chances to try again.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Knowing you had to cut ties with your parent to protect yourself doesn't make the holidays any easier. It's normal to miss having a family to celebrate with, feel guilty about not being together, or dread questions about why you're not seeing your parents. Even when you know you've made the right decision, the holidays can bring up feelings you thought you'd worked through.

Here's how to navigate the season in a way that protects your well-being and helps you regain some joy.

For many adult children of dysfunctional parents, holidays can be painful reminders of both your current reality and what you've lost. You may find yourself grieving the parent you're estranged from, but also the parent you always wished you'd had. It's completely natural to feel confused or upset; part of you may still long for a nurturing, loving connection, while another part knows that staying in a toxic relationship would only cause more pain.

Holidays can amplify these feelings because they're built around an idealized version of family that's never been your reality. You may feel pressure to attend gatherings that feel unsafe, or you may be flooded with painful memories when everyone around you seems to be celebrating. The goal is to learn to tolerate such feelings, knowing that they will lessen, and to treat yourself with compassion.

The first decision is whether to attend family events at all. This is always a choice, even when it doesn't feel like one. Choosing not to attend a gathering when your estranged parent will be there isn’t necessarily a sign of avoidance but of maintaining a boundary. If you do choose to attend, it should be because it genuinely serves you—and not because of guilt, obligation, or pressure from others.

Take time to weigh your options. Ask yourself: What's the emotional cost of attending? What do you hope to gain—and is it realistic? And will being there require you to compromise your boundaries or safety? (For people with abusive or toxic parents, skipping a holiday gathering may be the healthiest decision.)

Once you've made your decision, preparation can help you avoid reactive choices in an already emotional situation. Anxiety can build for days or weeks before a difficult holiday, so don't wait until the day arrives to think through your approach.

If you're not attending: Resist the pull to leave the day unstructured. A completely open day can intensify rumination and sadness. Plan something intentional that gives you something grounded to move toward.

If you're attending: Go in with a clear plan so you feel more grounded and in control.

Estrangement invites you to rethink what holidays can look like. You don't have to organize your life around traditions that cause pain; giving yourself permission to step away is progress in itself.

Think creatively about how you want to spend the holiday. Start new traditions, volunteer, or do something you genuinely enjoy but rarely make time for—a hike, a movie, or a good book. It's also completely fine to use the time to rest, reflect, practice self-care, do chores, or pursue hobbies. There are no rules: How you spend the day is completely up to you, whether that means making new meaning out of the holiday or simply getting through it in whatever way feels manageable.

Holidays can be emotionally draining, regardless of what you decide to do. In my book, Cutting Ties with Your Parents, I share these strategies for getting through the season:

Journaling is one of the most effective tools for working through complicated emotions; it slows your thinking and brings clarity. Try reflecting on questions like, What am I grieving today? What do I wish I'd received from my parents that I didn't? and What do I need right now, and how can I give it to myself?

If anxiety or distressing memories surface, try a grounding exercise, deep breathing, or a guided meditation to help interrupt the stress response.

Estrangement can’t erase the hurt you've experienced, but it can create space for healing. With each holiday you navigate, you may build more clarity about who you are, what you need, and what matters most to you. With practice, you’ll move from simply surviving the season to building traditions and relationships that feel safer, healthier, and more joyful.

#9418. Matching AI Modality To User Intent: Designing The Right Interface

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher at ServiceNow and the author of Design for the Mind (Manning, 2016) and the forthcoming Designing Agentic AI Experiences … More about Victor ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how users provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

To pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

Picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

While they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our users to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

The allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on users. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

When an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

A blank chat box creates a major problem for users who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

Designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

Having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

When an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

Imagine asking an AI for a project status update. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

The cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most important.

Before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

Designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for users with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

Table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

The following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

With this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

To choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:

The audit answers two questions for every feature:

Here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:

This is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because users often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

The Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

Interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

The Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-users and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

The Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

Once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

When you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your users.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

With Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

Choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Users might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status update only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

Table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

When teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve users whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

Field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

To address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

High-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

Second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

The resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

The AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

An AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

Start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

The future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

To get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

We focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

Use this worksheet during field observations. It allows design teams to document specific physical barriers before writing code.

Observe users as they perform a primary task in actual workspaces. Check all applicable conditions.

Rate the mental effort required to complete a specific workflow.

Chart user journeys across different environments. Document required input and output at each stage.

#9417. The Loneliness Trap

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

With unyielding inflation, economic uncertainty, and geopolitical friction sending collective anxiety levels higher and higher, many of us now consider genuine contentment an unaffordable luxury. Yet many decades of history serve as reminders that even amidst tremendous upheaval, human joy has never depended on what you can buy or external calm.

In this challenging environment, most of us want what we’ve always wanted: to be genuinely happy. Yet we are not willing to do what it takes to become happy.

A study from almost a century ago of the residents of the Northern English town of Bolton shows us the severe effects of not carving out time for our loved ones, a decision that most of us make every day. In the year my father was born, just over 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) to the east in Hungary, 1938—and then again in 2014—the residents of Bolton were asked what made them happy.

The most common ingredients of happiness among responses spanning 78 years were economic security and personal relationships, which were often tied together. Little mention was made of external events.

Joseph Roberts, a miner, despite answering the survey in 1938 when the threat of Hitler loomed large—the Nazi leader had already occupied Austria and parts of what was then Czechoslovakia—shared that what made him happy was returning from a day of hard work and spending time with his family.

“I see my kiddies and wife I am happy,” shared the miner. “When I am washed and romp with my kiddies, and when it is weekend and I tip up my humble wage and share with my wife in doling it out and we find we can manage another week we are happy. I am in regular work although it is hard and dangerous but I am happy because I have a contented mind.”

I am guessing you would agree that happiness is a seed you must grow in your life. Yet what most people do not understand is that you can’t grow your happiness alone; you can only do so with the help of others.

Since you cannot grow your happiness alone, it must also be true that happiness is a seed that grows in the gardens of others. How does this work?

We all seek happiness yet find it elusive. The reason is that most of us do not realize that one of the best ways to experience happiness is to help others experience it.

Plato understood this well. “Caring for the happiness of others,” observed the Greek philosopher over 2,500 years ago, “we find our own.”

Research also bears this out. Not only do people feel even more appreciated, happy, and connected to us than we expect them to when we give to them, but we also counterintuitively often benefit, as psychologists Sonja Lyubomirsky and Harry Reis note in their book How to Feel Loved, even more than they do.

I was reminded of this truth last month, when I spent nine days in a small town in rural Kenya where I had lived and worked as a Peace Corps volunteer 35 years earlier. Facilitating a pro bono leadership conference for rural primary and secondary school leaders and supporting five Kenyan women educators in teaching a women’s empowerment program for single mothers in one of Kenya’s most impoverished regions, I was struck by how happy I felt connecting with the people around me.

Returning to my comparatively more hermetic life of writing, researching, and teaching in Rome has been a jolt to my system; yet the memories remain and bring peace. In the end, I am like everyone else I’ve ever met in the world: traveling on an eternal search for connection and meaning.

Following the Italian way of expressing love, when you tell the other person “Ti voglio bene” (which means “I wish for your happiness”), you offer them the seed of happiness to plant in their own garden. You give them your support to grow in the way they desire, toward their own goals and values, or “to become,” as the former president of the American Psychological Association and the father of client-centered therapy, Carl Rogers, once wrote.

If the seed flourishes and becomes the flower of happiness, the other person may or may not bring you this flower one day. Sound risky? It may be; yet it’s the only way you will ever have the experience of seeing this flower in full bloom.

In other words, interconnectedness is the only path that will enable you to experience and sustain happiness throughout your life.

“Sounds good, Mr. Idealistic Author,” you may be thinking. “But how do I make daily decisions that will bring this interconnectedness into my life?”

If you want a more interconnected life, you will first have to ask yourself some tough questions about your daily decisions, right down to whether you should spend your time today ordering another gadget on Amazon or going hiking with a friend. Let’s consider this choice.

What do you think will bring you more happiness—an Amazon delivery or going on a hike with a friend? A study by Amit Kumar of the University of Texas has found that once you have a base level of financial resources, experiences rather than objects are the drivers of happiness.

Why? Experiences (“doing” something such as going to a meditation retreat or on a bicycle ride or to a restaurant or a concert) are more often shared, while objects (“owning” something such as a new shirt or book) are most often enjoyed alone.

In the end, the love we’ve shared with others is all we take with us. “All that we love deeply,” Helen Keller sagely observed, “becomes a part of us.” This is why experiences, which facilitate the sharing of love, produce much more long-term happiness than objects.

How, then, can you usher more happiness back into your life? Prioritize doing activities you enjoy in person with people you care about rather than buying objects to enjoy by your lonesome.

Just as you pursue objects to purchase and yet Prime shipping does not drop happiness at your doorstep, you also pursue social information about the people in your social network. As I write in my book Screened In, this search—like buying objects—does not bring the social connection that is the purveyor of genuine happiness into your life.

In sum, then, stop texting and call, go out with, see, visit, meet—in short, spend time with other, values-congruent people as often as you can.

In other words: Just. Connect. In person. In real time.

Spend time with the people you love, or could love if you were to get to know them better. Then happiness will cease to be a distant stranger and will become a part of your life again.

Specialising in AI, machine learning, and bespoke software products, SeidrLab’s ambition was to encapsulate their commitment to innovation, expertise, and forward-thinking approach.

Drawing inspiration from the ancient Norse art of Seidr, renowned for its prophecy and transformation, our team crafted a visual identity that reflected SeidrLab’s essence. #9415. Users Don’t Need More Tools: They Need Seamless Integrations

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

We often hear about shiny new tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

Users don’t get excited about shiny new “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and big design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

So no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, users can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

The instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

It’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where users want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

User’s value doesn’t emerge from users having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping users do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

Yet again, seamless integrations — a very underused but incredibly impactful way to deliver value fast, without adding the burden of installing and learning yet another tool.
